articles.title: Who is Nithya Raman, the democratic socialist who will be Los Angeles’s next mayor?
articles.summary: Urban planner and outsider who bested Karen Bass has close ties to Hollywood progressives – and a complicated relationship with the DSA
articles.body:
Nithya Raman on Thursday unseated Los Angeles mayor Karen Bass after a neck-and-neck race for the leadership for the US's second largest city.

The young progressive's victory means that the two largest cities in the US, as well the nation's capital, Washington DC, have now all elected democratic socialist mayors.

Though Raman's political ascendance in Los Angeles has sparked many comparisons to New York City's mayor Zohran Mamdani, her political profile in her home town is very different from Mamdani's, as is her often tense relationship with the local chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America.

Here's some key facts about LA's new mayor:

Raman broke into politics in 2020 by unseating an establishment Democrat on LA's powerful city council.

When Raman, an urban planner and political outsider, won a seat on LA's city council in 2020, it was the first time that a sitting city council member had been ousted in 17 years. One LA political analyst called her win "a political earthquake". Raman, whose campaign was endorsed by Bernie Sanders, was also the first DSA-endorsed candidate elected to office in Los Angeles. Raman credited her 2020 win to on-the-ground grassroots organizing, telling the Guardian at the time : "We knocked on 80,000 doors, which as far as we know, is a record. By the general election, we had 2,000 volunteers over all. We had 1,000 people just in our Slack."

She has close ties to Hollywood progressives, including an endorsement from the Hollywood writers' guild.

At the height of the #MeToo era, Raman served as the entertainment director for the Time's Up , the organization founded by powerful women in Hollywood that created a legal defense fund for women in all professions to fight back against pervasive sexual assault and sexual harassment.

While older Hollywood celebrities such as Jane Fonda and Samuel L Jackson endorsed Bass, Raman secured endorsements from younger celebrities and comedians such as Mindy Kaling, Adam Scott, and Jaboukie Young-White . Raman's husband, Vali Chandrasekaran, is a longtime TV writer .

She has also received attention from one very prominent celebrity Republican, former California governor Arnold Schwarzenegger, with whom she had " a widely publicized private meeting ".

Raman's key issues are housing policy, homelessness and tenants' rights.

Raman, an urban planner, has said she joined DSA-LA , which she did in 2019, not because of an " ideological drive ", but "because it was one of the only organizations that was meaningfully talking about housing affordability in the city". Her mayoral platform calls for building more housing "at all income levels, everything from deed-restricted affordable housing to market-rate housing to social housing to homeless shelters".

Her goal is to triple annual housing construction in the city, an approach that earned her an endorsement from advocacy group Yimby Action , which believes the best answer to housing affordability is simply building as much housing as possible.

Before she ran for office, Raman co-founded a still-active volunteer organization to help unhoused people in north-east LA.

In 2017, Raman was one of five co-founders of the SELAH Neighborhood Homeless Coalition , a group that organizes local volunteers in north-east LA to do outreach and advocacy with their unhoused neighbors. The group, which is still active and now claims 800 volunteers, is focused on recognizing "unhoused individuals as fellow members of our community worthy of the same dignity, respect and representation afforded to any housed person".

Raman won the mayoral race despite a conspicuous lack of support from her city council colleagues – even the fellow democratic socialists on the council.

In a mayoral debate with Raman, Bass, her opponent, brought up Raman's lack of support from other city council members and city leaders, saying: "Your colleagues have a very difficult time working with you." The three other democratic socialists who were elected to the LA city council after Raman all endorsed Bass for mayor .

"So the establishment doesn't like Raman: so what?" Los Angeles Times columnist Gustavo Arellano wrote , arguing that Raman's outsider status was precisely what voters frustrated with LA's Democratic political establishment wanted.

Raman, who was among the politicians revealed to have been targeted by establishment Democrats in the 2022 LA city hall audio tape leak scandal , won reelection to the city council in 2024 by a large margin.

At Raman's election night party, "the political class of Los Angeles was absent," Kurt Peterson, one of the leaders of hospitality union Unite Here local 11, which endorsed Raman, told Politico . But, he added: "Even though every city councilperson said they were standing with Karen Bass, not very many of the people they represent followed them to the polls."

While DSA-LA ultimately did endorse Raman for mayor, the endorsement was … complicated.

The local chapter of the DSA did not endorse Raman during the primary, when she entered the race at the last minute after previously endorsing Bass.

After she beat out reality star Spencer Pratt for second place and advanced into the runoff against Bass, DSA-LA did "enthusiastically" endorse her, but noted that "Councilmember Raman's relationship with DSA-LA, and the broader Angeleno grassroots left, has had some ups and downs". Among Raman's downs was "an inconsistent position on Palestine, which eventually resulted in conflict with the chapter over a 2024 endorsement from a pro-Israel Dem club", the group wrote in its voter guide , noting that they believed she had since "worked with us to improve on this issue".

But Raman's DSA-LA endorsement was almost rescinded in a vote of national DSA organizers over her stance on Israel, the Los Angeles Times reported , with a national political committee voting 14-13 against rescinding the local endorsement in early November.

Despite the endorsement drama, DSA-LA was quick to celebrate Raman's victory, posting a photo captioned, " YUP, that's our mayor !!!" even before the Associated Press had called the election in her favor.

Raman is proud of her willingness to break with allies and take 'unpopular' positions.

Raman touts her political independence – including her willingness to vote against her allies on key policy issues – as the heart of her political identity.

She broke with the DSA on her belief that LA's mansion tax, which brought in less revenue than supporters had hoped, needed to be reformed, which she called an "extremely unpopular sentiment".

One Hollywood comedian who supports Raman contrasted her with Mamdani by saying, "She's not ideological. She's a wonk," Vanity Fair reported.

Raman said she was "grateful" for comparisons to Mamdani, but "I am myself".

In recent interviews, Raman has emphasized her political distance from the DSA.

"The mayoral candidate said she favors the Scandinavian model of social democracy, signaling a belief in a regulated free-market economy rather than the more explicitly anti-capitalist vision embraced by many in the DSA," Vanity Fair wrote in an October profile .

Asked about comparisons to New York's democratic socialist mayor, Raman said : "Mamdani is one of the most popular politicians in America right now, and I'm very grateful to be compared to someone who is that skilled as a communicator and a leader. But I am different. I am myself."

articles.title: Trump says he’s declaring Oval Office and Cabinet Room national landmarks to prevent future changes
articles.summary: President Donald Trump signed a proclamation on Thursday that he said would designate the White House’s Oval Office and Cabinet Room as national landmarks —...
articles.body:
President Donald Trump signed a proclamation on Thursday that he said would designate the White House's Oval Office and Cabinet Room as national landmarks — a move he said would protect the two West Wing spaces from future changes.

The signing ceremony, which came on the heels of Republicans' stunning midterm losses on Tuesday, was his third event of the week related to his construction or renovation projects in the nation's capital — which have been largely unpopular with voters.

"It concerns the Oval Office and the Cabinet Room, very important spaces. And I'm going to be signing a document which will make them into a landmark for the ages," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office, which he's extensively gilded since returning to the White House in early 2025.

Trump said the administration would send the document to Congress.

"So we're going to be declaring it a national monument, and we're going to send it over to Congress, have it ratified," he said.

"It's a federal landmark — and when completed and when we get the documentation fully done, legally binding, it'll make it impossible for anybody ever to destroy this incredible space," he added.

CNN has reached out to the White House about the document and Trump's intentions.

Trump has put his distinctive imprint on the two White House spaces. In the Oval Office alone, he's added gold vermeil figurines on the mantle and medallions on the fireplace; gold eagles on the side tables; gilded Rococo mirrors on the doors; and, nestled in the pediments above the doorways, diminutive gold cherubs shipped in from Mar-a-Lago.

"I just thought it was very important that nobody be allowed to come in and take it down and try and do something with it," Trump added on Thursday.

This is a developing story and will be updated.

articles.title: Lula e ajuste fiscal: presidente alinha discurso com Durigan | G1
articles.summary: Lula reforça compromisso com o ajuste fiscal e a responsabilidade econômica ao alinhar propostas com Dario Durigan e afastar medidas consideradas de alto risco.
articles.body:
Após relutar em seguir o tempo do mercado, o presidente Lula fez os primeiros acenos concretos na direção de adotar um ajuste fiscal, comprometendo-se com responsabilidade fiscal e "economia arrumada" para atrair investimentos.

Ao mesmo tempo, afastou a possibilidade de adotar "fórmulas mágicas" e alinhou o discurso interno com as propostas do ministro da Fazenda, Dario Durigan.

Lula vai analisar medidas assim que voltar de sua viagem internacional à Turquia e Filipinas. Ele embarca na segunda-feira (9) e retorna na outra semana.

Até lá, os ministros Dario Durigan e Bruno Moretti (Planejamento) vão fechar as propostas que garantam o cumprimento do centro das metas fiscais, sem exceções, preservando os programas sociais e as promessas do presidente Lula.

Segundo participantes do encontro do presidente Lula com seus ministros, ex-ministros e economistas ligados ao PT desta quinta-feira (5), a "reunião foi produtiva", dissipou "dúvidas" que poderiam existir na cabeça de Lula e de seu vice, Geraldo Alckmin.

E também alinhou o discurso interno com as propostas que estão sendo defendidas pelo ministro Dario Durigan de perseguir o centro da meta fiscal, sem nenhum tipo de exceção, como pagamento de precatórios.

Durante a reunião no Palácio da Alvorada, a proposta do economista André Lara Resende , de fazer um plano para tabelar a taxa de juros e as metas fiscais, foi mencionada, mas descartada por ser considerada de alto risco num ano em que o país enfrentará desafios, como um crescimento menor e inflação pressionada pelo El Niño, combustíveis e entrada em vigor da nova escala de trabalho 5x2.

"A reunião foi produtiva, desanuviou as ideias do presidente e do vice sobre propostas mágicas e alinhou o discurso interno", disse um participante do encontro, acrescentando que o presidente deu sinal verde para que os ministro Dario Durigan e Bruno Moretti fechem as medidas para garantir superávit primário, sem exceções, mantendo todos os programas sociais.

Ao final do dia, depois de o presidente Lula também falar sobre responsabilidade fiscal em evento no Palácio do Planalto, a avaliação interna no governo é que o saldo da quinta-feira foi positivo, passando a mensagem para os investidores e economistas de que o Lula 4 fará o ajuste fiscal necessário para levar a uma redução da dívida pública.

No Planalto, Lula disse que vai trabalhar para ter uma economia "arrumada" , com responsabilidade fiscal e jurídica, na busca de atrair investimentos.

Segundo integrantes da reunião com o presidente, a fala dele no final do dia foi muito importante porque passou o recado de que ele terá responsabilidade fiscal, de que vai trabalhar para atrair investimentos e arrumar a casa.

Essa será a linha do pronunciamento do presidente no domingo (8) em cadeia aberta de rádio e TV , quando irá prometer pacificar o país, continuar reduzindo a pobreza no país e com responsabilidade fiscal para arrumar a economia brasileira.

A fala será genérica na economia, sem anúncio de medidas, mesmo porque elas ainda não estão fechadas, mas na direção de um ajuste na casa.

articles.title: Enem 2026: Aulão na Rede reúne centenas de alunos em Manaus | G1
articles.standfirst: Encontro foi uma oportunidade para os alunos revisarem os assuntos, tirarem dúvidas e reforçarem a confiança antes da prova.
articles.summary: Estudantes da rede pública de Manaus participam de revisão intensiva e tiram dúvidas no Aulão na Rede 2026 para garantir bom desempenho nas provas do Enem.
articles.body:
Aulão na Rede em Manaus — Foto: Jadson Lima/g1 AM

A dois dias do primeiro dia de provas do Exame Nacional do Ensino Médio (Enem) 2026, centenas de estudantes da rede pública participaram, na manhã desta sexta-feira (6), de uma revisão dos conteúdos cobrados no exame. O Aulão na Rede começou às 8h50, no Anfiteatro Ministro Bernardo Cabral, do Sesc Amazonas, no bairro Alvorada, Zona Centro-Oeste de Manaus .

O encontro foi uma oportunidade para os alunos revisarem os assuntos, tirarem dúvidas e reforçarem a confiança antes da prova. Para muitos, também foi uma forma de controlar a ansiedade na reta final dos estudos.

A estudante Rilary Roana, de 17 anos, que cursa o 3º ano do Ensino Médio, contou ao g1 que a preparação foi marcada por dificuldades. Segundo ela, o período de fumaça em Manaus prejudicou o andamento das aulas e afetou o aprendizado.

Na reta final, a estudante vê o aulão como uma oportunidade de reforçar os conhecimentos e diminuir o nervosismo. "A expectativa é alta, mas também é algo que dá um nervosismo bem grande, porque você não sabe se vai se sair bem. Com essa questão da fumaça, as aulas foram paradas e dificultaram o nosso aprendizado. Com esse Aulão na Rede, acredito que vai ajudar bastante, principalmente para a gente se acalmar um pouco mais em relação aos nervos para a prova", afirmou.

Rilary disse que ainda pretende revisar alguns conteúdos antes de domingo, mas sem manter um ritmo intenso de estudos. A prioridade será a redação, uma das etapas que exigem preparação dos candidatos.

A preocupação com a reta final também foi relatada por Gustavo Henrique, de 18 anos, aluno do 3º ano do Ensino Médio da Escola Zilda Arns Neumann. Ele saiu da Zona Leste de Manaus para participar do último Aulão na Rede antes do exame.

Segundo o estudante, os professores intensificaram a preparação nas últimas semanas, com simulados, resolução de questões e aulas voltadas às disciplinas cobradas no Enem.

Para ele, o encontro funciona como um reforço nos estudos e ajuda a diminuir a tensão antes da prova.

"O aulão dá mais um impulso para a gente. É mais um lugar para aprender e também para tirar um pouco desse nervosismo. Até então estou tranquilo. Quando chegar domingo, a gente vai ver", disse.

Preparação começou no início do ano letivo

Nas escolas, a preparação para o Enem começou meses antes da prova. A gestora da Escola Estadual Solon de Lucena, Joyce Pantoja, explicou ao g1 que os alunos participaram de simulados, exercícios e aulas de revisão ao longo do ano.

A escola tem aproximadamente 600 estudantes que estão concluindo o Ensino Médio. Segundo Joyce, o trabalho também envolve orientar os jovens sobre a importância do exame e as oportunidades de ingresso no ensino superior.

"É um momento em que eles vão colocar tudo aquilo que aprenderam durante esses três anos e realmente decidir o futuro deles. O Aulão na Rede fecha esse momento de preparação, mas é preciso que a escola passe o ano inteiro desenvolvendo atividades para que eles cheguem preparados para a prova", destacou.

A gestora também ressaltou a importância de orientar os estudantes sobre o funcionamento do exame. Neste ano, segundo ela, a pré-inscrição realizada pelo Ministério da Educação ( MEC ) facilitou a participação dos alunos.

Para ajudar nesse processo, a escola promoveu um mutirão para que os estudantes acessassem o portal Gov.br e validassem as informações.

O Aulão na Rede 2026 é uma iniciativa do Grupo Rede Amazônica e da Fundação Rede Amazônica, com patrocínio da Uninorte e apoio institucional do Sesc e da Evolução. A Secretaria de Estado de Educação e Desporto Escolar (Seduc) participa da organização e da mobilização dos estudantes da rede estadual.

A programação inclui revisão das quatro áreas do conhecimento cobradas no Enem: Linguagens, Ciências Humanas, Ciências Exatas e Ciências da Natureza. Os participantes também recebem apostilas para acompanhar as aulas e consultar os conteúdos depois.

O encontro presencial encerra um mês de preparação promovido pelo projeto. Durante outubro, dicas foram exibidas nos telejornais da Rede Amazônica e videoaulas foram disponibilizadas pelo g1 .

articles.title: Fazenda: ajuste fiscal sem estelionato eleitoral | G1
articles.standfirst: Presidente busca um “caminho estreito” entre o corte de despesas e a preservação da agenda social; escolha do comando da Fazenda passa pela capacidade de conciliar política e mercado
articles.summary: O ajuste fiscal governo Lula busca conter gastos sem romper promessas sociais, enquanto nomes como Alckmin e Durigan surgem para comandar o Ministério da Fazenda.
articles.body:
A avaliação entre interlocutores de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ( PT ) é que o início do quarto mandato exigirá um ajuste fiscal, com ênfase na contenção e revisão de despesas, mas sem caracterizar um estelionato eleitoral.

O compromisso é preservar os benefícios e programas sociais defendidos durante a campanha, evitando qualquer sinalização de que o governo pretende descumprir suas promessas.

Um plano será apresentado em algum momento. A decisão de não antecipar medidas ou metas é estratégica: o governo não quer criar expectativas que, caso não sejam integralmente atendidas, provoquem frustração e reação negativa do mercado.

A escolha do futuro ministro da Fazenda está diretamente vinculada a esse plano. O ministro terá a missão de equilibrar as demandas da rua e da Faria Lima, fazendo a interlocução política e econômica e transformando o ajuste em medidas concretas.

“Não há vários cenários sobre a mesa. Há um caminho estreito”

Dario Durigan : tem trânsito com o mercado financeiro, experiência na Fazenda e interlocução com Lula.

Rafael Fonteles: governador do Piauí, com experiência na área econômica.

Camilo Santana : nome político de confiança de Lula.

Geraldo Alckmin : alternativa de peso político e credibilidade, mas com um obstáculo institucional: sendo vice-presidente, não poderia ser afastado do governo como um ministro comum em caso de crise.

O dilema é encontrar alguém com autoridade política, interlocução com o mercado e capacidade de executar um ajuste delicado, sem comprometer as promessas eleitorais.

articles.title: INSS muda regras do auxílio-doença sem perícia e cria reanálise após benefício negado | G1
articles.standfirst: Segurado terá 10 dias para pedir nova análise e poderá apresentar outros documentos médicos. Após duas negativas seguidas, novos pedidos serão encaminhados para perícia.
articles.summary: Segurado terá 10 dias para pedir nova análise e poderá apresentar outros documentos médicos. Após duas negativas seguidas, novos pedidos serão encaminhados para perícia.
articles.body:
O Ministério da Previdência Social e o Instituto Nacional do Seguro Social (INSS) mudaram as regras para a concessão do auxílio por incapacidade temporária, o antigo auxílio-doença , por meio da análise de documentos médicos, sem perícia presencial.

Com a mudança, o segurado que tiver o benefício negado por parecer técnico na análise dos documentos poderá pedir uma reanálise em até 10 dias , contados a partir da ciência da decisão. Nessa etapa, poderá apresentar novos documentos médicos ou odontológicos.

A mudança consta de portaria conjunta publicada no Diário Oficial da União (DOU) desta sexta-feira (6) e já está em vigor.

A norma também determina que, depois de dois indeferimentos seguidos pela análise documental, os pedidos posteriores sejam encaminhados obrigatoriamente para perícia médica.

A reanálise vale para os casos em que o benefício é negado por parecer técnico na análise documental.

Com a alteração, o segurado poderá solicitar a reanálise da documentação médica antes de recorrer da decisão.

O prazo será de dez dias após o segurado tomar ciência da negativa. A análise ficará a cargo da Perícia Médica Federal. O trabalhador também poderá usar essa oportunidade para apresentar novos documentos médicos ou odontológicos.

Segundo a portaria, se o segurado optar por entrar diretamente com recurso enquanto ainda estiver correndo o prazo de dez dias para a reanálise, perderá a possibilidade de pedir essa nova avaliação.

Já para quem solicitar a reanálise, o prazo para entrar com recurso começará a contar a partir da ciência da decisão sobre o novo pedido.

As novas regras valem para as negativas comunicadas aos segurados a partir desta sexta.

Aplicativo "Meu INSS" — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

Após duas negativas, pedido vai para perícia

O governo também alterou a regra para quem recebe sucessivas negativas na análise documental.

A partir de agora, após dois indeferimentos consecutivos, os requerimentos seguintes deverão ser encaminhados obrigatoriamente para agendamento de exame médico-pericial.

A perícia poderá ser presencial ou feita por telemedicina, desde que o segurado cumpra os requisitos para esse tipo de atendimento.

Essa exigência continuará valendo para os pedidos seguintes até que haja eventual concessão de benefício por incapacidade por meio de perícia presencial ou por telemedicina.

A análise documental é feita pelo chamado Atestmed, sistema que permite ao segurado pedir o auxílio por incapacidade temporária apresentando documentos médicos, sem a necessidade imediata de uma perícia presencial. O pedido pode ser feito pelo site ou aplicativo Meu INSS, com o envio de atestados e exames complementares.

O auxílio por incapacidade temporária, também conhecido como auxílio-doença, é destinado a trabalhadores segurados pelo INSS que ficam temporariamente impossibilitados de trabalhar em razão de doença ou outra condição de saúde.

As regras do Atestmed foram reformuladas neste ano. Em março, o governo ampliou de 60 para até 90 dias o período máximo de afastamento que pode ser concedido por meio da análise documental. Segundo o governo, a medida buscava reduzir a demanda pelas perícias presenciais e ajudar a diminuir a fila do INSS.

Em setembro, o Ministério da Previdência e o INSS prorrogaram por mais 365 dias a regra que permite a concessão do benefício por até 90 dias por meio da análise documental.

Para que o pedido seja analisado, os documentos médicos devem estar legíveis e sem rasuras . Também precisam conter informações como identificação do segurado, data de emissão, tempo estimado de afastamento, diagnóstico ou código da Classificação Internacional de Doenças (CID) e identificação do profissional responsável.

As regras do Atestmed vêm passando por mudanças após cobranças do Tribunal de Contas da União (TCU).

Entre as determinações estavam a adoção de mecanismos para verificar a autenticidade dos atestados , a organização de dados relevantes sobre os profissionais responsáveis pelos documentos e o reforço dos controles internos.

O TCU também determinou providências para garantir a avaliação da efetiva incapacidad e do segurado e a definição do período adequado de afastamento, além da possibilidade de negar o pedido quando houver indícios de fraude ou falta de direito ao benefício.

articles.title: Pete Hegseth strikes defiant tone in face of impeachment threat
articles.summary: Many lawmakers, including some Republicans, have criticized the defense secretary over his handling of the Iran war.
articles.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Thursday dismissed a renewed effort in the House to bring articles of impeachment against him as early as next week.

In a video on social media , Hegseth said, "A disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly, just like they tried against President Trump twice."

Hegseth was referring to Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., who said Wednesday that he plans to reintroduce articles of impeachment when the House is back in session. Lawmakers are scheduled to return to Washington on Monday.

"It's all about the politics of personal destruction," Hegseth added. "Didn't work against President Trump, and it won't work with me. You can rest assured of that."

In the more-than-five-minute video, Hegseth only briefly touched on the Iran war — a driving force behind the effort to impeach him, as well as GOP losses in this week's midterm elections.

Massie, who lost his GOP primary after he crossed Trump, urged Trump on Thursday to replace Hegseth while he still has a GOP majority in the Senate.

"My Hegseth impeachment resolution is a much gentler version of what's coming when Dem's control Congress. They'll have hearings & trials," he said on X .

"There is one contingency in which I won't reintroduce the articles of impeachment: Hegseth resigns," Massie wrote Wednesday .

Numerous Democrats have indicated a desire to oust Hegseth since their midterm election wins, including House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York , who is poised to be the next speaker.

Trump said Wednesday that he is not planning to replace Hegseth, and he said Thursday that Hegseth "has done a fantastic job" and "probably has opposition" over the actions he has taken, including purging military leadership.

Trump has told some allies he is considering replacing Hegseth, asking them who they think should succeed him, two people familiar with discussions told NBC News this week. He has previously insisted that he was not considering dismissing department heads just days before they were shown the door.

Massie tried to force a vote on impeaching Hegseth in September, but his efforts were stunted when House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., sent the House home early.

He would need several Republicans to join all Democrats in supporting the impeachment measure for it to succeed.

The House has impeached only two Cabinet officials in history — former President Joe Biden's homeland security secretary, Alejandro Mayorkas, in a partisan vote, and William Belknap, the secretary of war in the 1870s. No Cabinet members have ever been convicted by the Senate.

articles.title: Republicans rammed through Supreme Court nominees. Now Democrats will have the votes to stop them
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump led a transformation of the Supreme Court that ushered in a conservative supermajority but soon he will confront an...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump led a transformation of the Supreme Court that ushered in a conservative supermajority but soon he will confront an emboldened Democratic-led Senate that is preparing to play hardball on his judicial nominations.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, who is likely to return as majority leader next year, promised in an interview with The Associated Press that Democrats will prevent the Republican president from installing a "right-winger" on the Supreme Court and that they are "not going to allow any crappy nominees" elsewhere in the federal judiciary or in Trump's Cabinet.

Democrats will hold at least 54 seats in the 100-member Senate next year and as many as 56 depending on final results in Mississippi and Alaska, giving them a significant majority to block Trump's nominees or just ignore them outright.

After years of being on the losing end of highly partisan confirmation fights against Republicans, especially on Supreme Court nominees, Democrats will be under considerable pressure to wield the same type of aggressive tactics.

This all but erases any prospect that Trump could add to his imprint on the court he established in his first term by naming three of the current justices. In the past, Trump had mused privately that he could end up nominating up to seven people for the nine-person bench by the end of his second term, according to a person with knowledge of those comments.

Schumer declined to say specifically whether he would hold any Supreme Court vacancy open until after the next presidential election, as former Senate Republican leader Mitch McConnell did in 2016 , clearing the way for Trump to nominate the first of his three Supreme Court picks.

"The bottom line is, we're not going to allow a right-winger on the court," Schumer said.

The White House said Thursday that "extreme Democrats have a history of politicizing the Supreme Court, even entertaining plans to pack the Court with liberal justices."

"President Trump will never let them pack the Supreme Court and ruin the independent judiciary," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said.

Neither of the court's two oldest justices, Samuel Alito, 76, or Clarence Thomas, 78, has publicly indicated an imminent retirement. Lifetime appointments typically come with a remove from political upheaval, even of the scale of Tuesday's elections in which Democrats regained control of both the House and the Senate .

"I think the justices must know that if they were to retire now, at this moment, right before Democrats take the Senate, there would be an enormous amount of pressure unlike any we've seen to make serious change to the court," said Dale Carpenter, a law professor at Southern Methodist University's law school.

Alito has publicly mused about retirement in recent months, telling The Associated Press that he's not sure "how long I'll be able to continue to do this job." But he's also said he'll stay on the court through the end of the term next summer and told Bloomberg he would not step down during a lame-duck period.

Meanwhile, Thomas is closing in on a record-setting tenure and would become the longest-serving justice in the nation's history if he served until May 2028.

Trump has shown unusual deference to Alito and Thomas, even as he's attacked other justices who've ruled against him, praising both for their legal acumen and declining to say whether they should step down so the president could nominate their successors.

In a Fox News Channel interview in April, Trump said he has a shortlist of potential nominees but said he did not know whether he would have another vacancy this year, citing Alito's "very good physical health."

The Democrats' sizable margins in the Senate also will hamper the Republicans' effort to regain ground in the 2028 elections, in which the GOP will be defending states such as Wisconsin, North Carolina and Iowa where Democrats made significant gains on Tuesday.

"Chance of confirming a worthy successor to Justice Thomas and/or Alito during President Trump's term: Zero," Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis posted on X after Tuesday's elections. "Chance of confirming a worthy successor during a hypothetical GOP admin 2029-2033: probably zero (GOP won't be able to recapture enough seats in 28)."

Historically, some justices have timed their retirements with the president who would name their successor in mind, but it's far from the only consideration in their decision-making.

Former liberal Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg famously resisted efforts from progressives to retire when President Barack Obama, a Democrat, was in office and died in the last year of Trump's first term, allowing him to replace her with conservative Justice Amy Coney Barrett .

Barrett would go on in 2022 to join the majority opinion in Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization, which erased the constitutional right to an abortion .

Even if there were a surprise Supreme Court vacancy in the coming weeks, lame-duck confirmations while Republicans still remain in power aren't a sure thing.

Trump effectively forced Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina out of a reelection bid. That seat was won Tuesday by one of the state's former governors, Democrat Roy Cooper. The president also opposed two Republican incumbents in their primary races, Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana and Sen. John Cornyn of Texas. Democrats flipped the seat in Texas. Maine Sen. Susan Collins, another Republican who lost, attributed her defeat in part to Trump.

articles.title: Trump admin sues Penn State over in-state tuition policy for undocumented migrants
articles.summary: The DOJ's lawsuit accuses Pennsylvania State University of offering undocumented students in-state tuition rates that discriminate against U.S. citizens.
articles.body: The Trump administration is suing Pennsylvania State University over a policy that allegedly allows undocumented migrant students to qualify for in-state tuition. In a lawsuit filed on Thursday, the Justice Department argued that in-state tuition for undocumented migrants discriminates against U.S. citizens because U.S. citizens living outside Pennsylvania are not eligible for the same reduced tuition rate. "Congress made a deliberate policy choice that states and their public institutions may not grant tuition benefits to illegal aliens unless those same benefits are made to all U.S. citizens," Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate of the DOJ's Civil Division said in a statement. "This university has ignored that mandate. The Department will continue to challenge policies that unlawfully disadvantage American citizens," he continued. JUSTICE DEPARTMENT SUES COLORADO OVER IN-STATE TUITION AND FINANCIAL AID FOR ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS The DOJ accused the university of violating federal law by "prioritizing the needs of illegal aliens over U.S. citizens in defiance of Congress’s commands." Penn State's policy "unconstitutionally" discriminates against U.S. citizens who are not afforded the same reduced tuition rate as undocumented students, the department said. The department seeks to enjoin the university from enforcing its policy that provides undocumented students, including illegal migrants who live in Pennsylvania, with in-state tuition rates, regardless of whether the students are lawfully in the U.S. DOJ SUES NEW JERSEY OVER LAWS GIVING ILLEGAL ALIENS IN-STATE TUITION, SAYS CITIZENS TREATED AS 'SECOND-CLASS' The complaint also aims to enjoin the institution from adopting any new tuition policies that favor undocumented students over U.S. citizens. According to Penn State's website, undocumented students with or without Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) status may be eligible for in-state tuition if they meet certain residency requirements. "These requirements include attending an accredited Pennsylvania high school for at least four years and graduating from an accredited Pennsylvania high school or receiving a Pennsylvania General Educational Development (GED) certificate," the school's website reads. FOX News Digital has reached out to the university for comment on the DOJ's lawsuit. "The Department of Justice today continues its efforts to ensure that no state law or university policy gives preferential treatment to illegal aliens over our Nation’s own citizens," Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward, Jr. said in a statement. "Congress long ago made clear that states, through their public universities, cannot give reduced tuition to illegal aliens not available to all Americans."

articles.title: Midterm wave sets a course for "Medicare for All" fight
articles.summary: Voter frustration with healthcare costs helped fuel the Democrats' midterm takeover of Congress. But Democratic control doesn't mean "Medicare for All" will...
articles.body:
LANSING, Mich. — Fifteen years working as an emergency room nurse has convinced Kim Bogan that the only way to fix the American healthcare system is to tear it down and start over.

Her patients arriving for triage are sicker than ever. They can't afford many of the prescriptions they get in the ER. And sometimes when patients die, she wonders if she could have saved them had she not been caring for five or six other people at once.

That's why she spent the past year shuttling between 12-hour shifts at this city's Sparrow Hospital and campaigning for Abdul El-Sayed , the Democrat who made "Medicare for All" a signature issue in his congressional campaign and is now a senator-elect.

But she realizes that just because progressive candidates successfully campaigned on some form of the policy in states such as Texas, Iowa, Maine, and Michigan, it doesn't mean Medicare for All will be an easy sell. "Nobody expected that," Bogan said.

Medicare for All typically refers to a government health program that would guarantee Americans coverage by replacing most or all private insurance. Critics are already pointing out that, even in a blue wave as massive as the 2026 midterms , the most vocal Medicare for All champions generally won by smaller margins than more moderate Democrats.

"Whatever else people voted for in this midterm election — anger about inflation, anger about corruption, anger about the Iran war — they by and large didn't vote to have the government take over health insurance," said Jonathan Oberlander , a professor and healthcare reform expert at the University of North Carolina-Chapel Hill.

Still, supporters of universal healthcare see this moment as a once-in-a-generation opportunity because Americans are buckling under the weight of healthcare costs and are hungry for change. Several states, including Oregon , are already exploring what it would take to set up single-payer systems.

The affordability crisis "dominated this election, and Medicare for All speaks to that," Oberlander said. Medicare for All supporters expect the policy agenda will gain major momentum heading into the 2028 Democratic presidential primaries, he said.

But more moderate Democrats may see the idea's growing popularity as a threat to gains they made in states such as Iowa, Kansas, and South Carolina. "If Democrats want to hold those seats, which were very difficult to win, they're probably not interested in passing Medicare for All," Oberlander said. "That's a huge political risk in red-leaning states. So just because Democrats have a majority doesn't mean it's a majority for Medicare for All."

Previous Medicare for All proposals would have required getting millions of people to willingly give up their existing coverage, fueling unprecedented opposition from the healthcare industry, said Michael Cannon , a healthcare economist at the libertarian Cato Institute and a Medicare for All opponent.

"If Medicare for All actually had the price levels that Bernie Sanders and Abdul El-Sayed envision, the industry would tear it to shreds," he said.

And even as voters say they support Medicare for All in greater numbers than in nearly a decade, support falters when they're presented with common arguments against it — like it could lead to higher taxes or delays in treatment — according to a recent KFF poll.

Jaime Bardenhagen said she feels a little guilty about the idea of getting her healthcare coverage from the government. A former nurse in rural Leelanau County in northern Michigan, Bardenhagen has Parkinson's and sialidosis, a rare genetic disease that can cause seizures.

Yet she "feels bad" about qualifying for disability benefits next year. Such programs were something she "didn't believe in" while growing up on a farm, she said. You were supposed to work for what you needed, she said, not rely on government support. "And I did work as hard as I could, for as long as I could."

But like millions of Americans, Bardenhagen and her husband saw their health insurance costs skyrocket this year, after the Affordable Care Act enhanced subsidies expired.

Their monthly premiums went from $700 to $1,300, with a deductible of $7,500. They started putting off medical tests her doctor wanted, she said. "We couldn't afford that," she said.

Her husband voted for Donald Trump in 2016, Bardenhagen said. This time, he stayed home. Bardenhagen, a Democrat, also considered sitting out the midterms. "I just don't trust either party anymore," she said.

Despite those misgivings, she says she supports Medicare for All. Her years as a nurse left her disillusioned with the current healthcare system, she said.

She felt the insurance companies, not doctors, were calling the shots, determining which prescriptions and procedures patients could receive. Wouldn't it be fairer, she figured, if "good people" in government were making those calls? "So, absolutely, the government should take it over."

That takeover is Cannon's worst-case scenario. The libertarian economist said giving the federal government greater control over the healthcare system would only backfire. Patients would be left "in even more vulnerable positions, because they would be relying for their access to healthcare on government spending that is just not sustainable."

Medicare for All supporters are naive to think the government could negotiate lower drug and healthcare prices by replacing private plans with a public one, he said. "Everyone knows that the industry is going to end up running the show, and that has been the case since they passed Medicare," Cannon said.

For Bardenhagen, the former nurse in northern Michigan, the message she wants Democrats to take from the midterms is simple: "Do something," she said.

"With the election results, both parties are going to be under pressure to come up with solutions to address the current affordability crisis in healthcare," said Sara Collins , a senior scholar at the Commonwealth Fund, a private foundation that supports healthcare research.

That could mean smaller, but still significant, bipartisan deals that might have seemed unthinkable before the midterms: things such as reinstating the enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies that expired at the end of last year, or other measures with broad support, such as curbing insurance companies' use of prior authorizations, which requires patients to get insurers' approval before proceeding with a covered treatment.

"That's probably the lowest-hanging fruit for them, I'd think," said Patricia Votava, a political strategist based in Sullivan's Island, South Carolina.

The pressure for healthcare reform is likely to grow, too, with Affordable Care Act premiums set to rise by double digits again next year; employers passing on more of their growing insurance premium costs to workers; and massive cuts to Medicaid looming , which are projected to leave 7.5 million more people uninsured by 2034.

On the whole, the midterm results could push Democrats' healthcare agenda further left, Oberlander said. Some Democrats could support a public option, a government-backed health plan people could opt into. Others in the party could coalesce around a version of Medicare for All that doesn't fully replace private insurance but serves as "guaranteed baseline government health insurance," as El-Sayed described his current plan in the campaign .

"If you like your insurance from your employer or from your union, that can still be there for you," he said.

Whatever they opt for, Democrats shouldn't expect voters to be willing to wait patiently for years of gradual change, Oberlander said. "If the window opens, you better jump right through."

South Carolina correspondent Lauren Sausser contributed to this report.

articles.title: Somali daycare owner tied to fraud wins Minnesota House race sparking online fury: 'Lost state'
articles.summary: Abdi Daisane's Blooming Kids Child Care Center in St. Cloud received millions in state and federal funding and has faced multiple violations.
articles.body: ST. CLOUD, Minn. — The owner of a Somali daycare center that has faced scrutiny over state and federal funding and is linked to a massive fraud settlement won a seat in the Minnesota legislature Tuesday night. Minnesota Democratic–Farmer–Labor Party (DFL) candidate Abdi Daisane defeated a Republican incumbent to win Minnesota’s House District 14A seat in St. Cloud, Minnesota, becoming the first Somali-born lawmaker in the statehouse from St. Cloud, MPR News reported. Daisane, who delivered part of his victory speech in Somali, is the CEO of Blooming Kids Child Care Center in St. Cloud, which has received $7.29 million from the state-run Child Care Assistance Program since 2018. His childcare business also received $598,251.62 from the federally-funded Child and Adult Care Food Program (CACFP) since 2020. A nonprofit called Partners in Nutrition, which recently had to pay an $18.5 million civil settlement for fraud, was the center's sponsor for CACFP funds. A press release from the settlement says Partners in Nutrition "knowingly defrauded the State of Minnesota out of millions of dollars in federal child nutrition funds during and after the COVID-19 pandemic, in violation of the Minnesota False Claims Act." MINNESOTA OFFICIAL'S VOTER GUIDE MESSAGE ON SOMALI TV TRIGGERS VIRAL BACKLASH: 'NOT AN ACCIDENT' Fox News Digital visited Blooming Kids Child Care Center on Thursday and found a quiet scene. The childcare center is situated along a main road in St. Cloud's small downtown. A paper sign on a wooden front door that faces the street directs visitors to a different entrance. The floor-to-ceiling glass windows next to the door are covered with a tinted and mirrored film. The building is flanked by a parking lot that was mostly empty on Thursday afternoon. Behind the building is a tiny fenced-in playground, anchored by two children's jungle gyms that appear to fill most of the area. Alpha News reported on the funding in late October, and spoke with a nearby worker who said they never saw children entering or exiting the childcare facility. The outlet also reported that Blooming Kids Child Care Center has been cited for over a dozen violations. Additionally, questions about the immigration status of Daisane's wife, Ayaan Aydid, have circulated online after a video surfaced of her detailing to the BBC how she crossed into the United States at the southern border. CULTURE CLASH LAID BARE AS VIOLENT SOMALI GANGS GRIP SUBURBAN COMMUNITIES: ‘THESE KIDS ARE DIFFERENT’ Daisane did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. News of Daisane’s victory quickly sparked pushback on social media. "We are a lost state," Red Ax Strategies President Matt Brodsky posted on X. "We should cede it to Canada." "MINNESOTA IS SO FREAKING COOKED," conservative commentator Eric Daugherty posted on X. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Minnesota is done," conservative personality Gunther Eagleman posted. ACT for America founder Bridgette Gabriel flagged a post about Daisane's election — and his purported illegal immigrant wife — to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin on X. "[G]reat opportunity to do something about this," she said.

Daisane did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

News of Daisane's victory quickly sparked pushback on social media.

"We are a lost state," Red Ax Strategies President Matt Brodsky posted on X . "We should cede it to Canada."

"MINNESOTA IS SO FREAKING COOKED," conservative commentator Eric Daugherty posted on X.

"Minnesota is done," conservative personality Gunther Eagleman posted .

ACT for America founder Bridgette Gabriel flagged a post about Daisane's election — and his purported illegal immigrant wife — to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin on X.

"[G]reat opportunity to do something about this," she said .

articles.title: TED JENKIN: Democrats took Congress. Don’t let your emotions make bad money moves
articles.summary: Your 401(k) doesn't have a political affiliation, and history shows why making emotional investment decisions after midterm elections can backfire.
articles.body: Democrats have taken control of the House and Senate. President Donald Trump remains in the White House. Republicans are furious. Democrats are celebrating. And millions of Americans are staring at their retirement accounts wondering one thing: What the heck does this mean for my 401(k)? Should you sell stocks? Buy gold? Move everything into cash? Before you make a move, you might want to look at what history actually tells us. Because this particular combination of political power has produced some surprising stock market results. STATE OF PLAY: BLUE WAVE SWEEPS DEMOCRATS INTO POWER, WITH KEY RACES STILL HANGING IN BALANCE The worst political combination for stocks? According to research from RBC Wealth Management and Bloomberg, the S&P 500 has historically averaged just 4.9% annually when a Republican president faces a Democratic-controlled House and Senate. That's the lowest average among six political configurations studied from 1953 through 2025. Compare that with the other combinations: TRUMP PLEDGES TO VETO 'INSANE' DEM BILLS, PINPOINTS ISSUE PARTIALLY TO BLAME FOR REPUBLICAN LOSSES Those are historical annual price returns, excluding dividends, not predictions for 2027. But here's what should catch your attention. Not all political gridlock has produced the same stock market results. And anyone telling you Wall Street always loves divided government isn't looking at the complete numbers. But here's the midterm surprise Before you start selling everything in your retirement account, there's another statistic you need to know. According to Capital Group, the S&P 500 has averaged a 15.4% gain in the 12 months following midterm elections since 1950. Even more remarkable? Every post-midterm 12-month period in that study produced a positive return. That's a pretty impressive historical batting average. Why? DEMOCRATS' HISTORIC WINS IN TEXAS HIGHLIGHT TAKING CONTROL OF CONGRESS IN MIDTERM BLUE WAVE One explanation is that markets dislike uncertainty. Before elections, investors worry about taxes, regulations, spending and which party will control Washington. Once the election is over, some of that uncertainty disappears. Wall Street may not like the election results, but it often likes knowing the results. Gridlock isn't always good for your money When Democrats control Congress and Trump controls the White House, passing major legislation generally becomes more difficult. Tax changes require negotiation. Spending bills can become political battlegrounds. Government shutdowns and debt-ceiling fights can create uncertainty. Some investors welcome the reduced likelihood of sweeping policy changes. Others worry that Washington won't be able to address serious fiscal challenges. But remember something important: The stock market doesn't rise or fall simply because politicians agree or disagree. Corporate profits, inflation, interest rates and economic growth still drive long-term investment performance. And historical political averages don't prove that congressional control caused those returns. Four things I'd watch in 2027 First, corporate earnings. Companies making more money can support higher stock prices regardless of who's running Congress. Second, interest rates. Federal Reserve decisions and inflation could have a much bigger impact on your portfolio than congressional gridlock. Will we see another two or three rate hikes if inflation stays stubborn? WHAT THE 2026 MIDTERM RESULTS MEAN FOR CAPITOL HILL Third, taxes. Major changes to corporate, capital gains or individual income taxes would face significant political hurdles. Fourth, government spending and debt. Budget battles could affect Treasury yields, borrowing costs and investor confidence. We are still more than $40 trillion in debt. According to research from RBC Wealth Management and Bloomberg, the S&P 500 has historically averaged just 4.9% annually when a Republican president faces a Democratic-controlled House and Senate. These are the issues that can actually affect your financial future. Don't let your politics destroy your portfolio I've spent decades watching investors make one of the biggest mistakes in personal finance. They confuse political disappointment with investment strategy. They sell stocks because they dislike the president. They move into cash because they dislike Congress. Then they wait for an election result that makes them comfortable. Meanwhile, the stock market keeps moving. Here's the reality: A 4.9% historical average doesn't mean your portfolio will earn 4.9% in 2027. And a 15.4% post-midterm average doesn't guarantee a rally. History gives us perspective, not a crystal ball. If you're retiring next year, make sure your portfolio can handle volatility. If retirement is 20 years away, don't let one election derail a long-term investment strategy. Because here's the most important financial lesson from this election. Your 401(k) doesn't have a political affiliation. It doesn’t vote red or blue, it’s always voting green. articles.title: Not Trump's fault? Sarah Huckabee Sanders on the midterm blame game
articles.summary: Stay all in with Trump or create some distance? The freshly reelected Arkansas governor on a debate that is starting in the GOP.
articles.body:
Sarah Huckabee Sanders isn't one of those Republicans, many in states formerly known as red, who found themselves ousted from office in the midterm elections. But the freshly re-elected Arkansas governor does have some thoughts on what went wrong in the GOP.

Was it President Donald Trump ? Not his fault, she says.

"I think each race has to be looked at independently, and the president, while he still remains the most influential voice in all of Republican politics − frankly, in all of politics − his name wasn't on the ballot," she said in an exclusive interview with USA TODAY about her new book, "Unapologetic," published Nov. 10 by St. Martin's Press. "And so I don't think that this can be a line drawn against him."

Actually, just about every independent analyst and a fair share of those in the GOP do blame Trump for losses that cost Republicans control of the House and the Senate and a majority of governorships. Exit polls of voters showed that dissatisfaction with the president, especially over the economy, propelled Democratic victories in such unlikely places as Texas and Kansas and South Carolina.

Candidates make history in race, gender and faith in 2026

But her defense does put Sanders − who served as White House press secretary for Trump in his first term − squarely in the all-in-for-Trump lane of the approaching debate about the GOP's future.

Even Vice President JD Vance struck a different tone in his autopsy of the midterms, putting a bit of distance between himself and his boss. "The reason we lost is the war" in Iran, Vance said i n a lengthy post on the social-media platform X the day after the election. "If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so."

That was not an argument Vance went on to make. But Sanders did.

"I'm thankful that we have a president who is willing to stand up and do sometimes what is not easy, what is not always politically convenient, but what is certainly in the interest of the American people," she said, noting Iran's nuclear ambitions and its support of terrorism. "I'm thankful that we had a president that was willing to take that on" despite the "negative" economic consequences, including higher gas prices.

Her father, former Arkansas governor Mike Huckabee , is a key player in the administration's Mideast policy as the U.S. ambassador to Israel .

"The president continues to be the most influential voice not just in the Republican Party but in all of politics," she repeated. "I don't think that's changing anytime soon."

Just to be clear, writing a book touting your record in office and publishing it as a presidential campaign is getting into gear is generally seen as a declaration of political ambition for bigger things.

Ask Jimmy Carter ("Why Not the Best?") or Barack Obama ("The Audacity of Hope"), both of whom went on to win their White House bids in 1976 and 2008, respectively. This year alone, books have sprouted from California Gov. Gavin Newsom ("Young Man in a Hurry") and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro ("Where We Keep the Light") and Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (Go and Do Likewise").

Vance has one, too. "Communion: Finding My Way Back to Faith," published in June , tells the story of his spiritual journey to Catholicism .

Faith of the Baptist variety is threaded through Sanders' book, "Unapologetic: Clarity and Conviction in a World Gone Crazy." In it, she discusses the central importance of her faith in her personal life and her professional one.

She opens the book with an account of the jarring diagnosis of thyroid cancer in the middle of her first campaign for governor four years ago, and the successful 6-1/2-hour surgery to remove it. She champions her record in Arkansas of cutting taxes and revamping education, including an improvement in student test scores. There are affectionate anecdotes about her husband, political consultant Bryan Sanders, and their three children, Scarlett, Huck and George.

Sarah Huckabee Sanders is, she notes, the first mom to serve as White House press secretary, the first woman to be elected governor of Arkansas, and, at age 44, the youngest governor in the country.

Would she like to add the first woman president to her resume?

"I think everybody wants to rush into four years from now," she responded, laughing. "We're not even four days past the last election. I'm going to continue to keep my focus where it needs to be, and that's right here at home, doing the job I was just elected to have."

Neither was her response when asked if she would make a commitment to serve all four years of that new term.

"I certainly hope I have no reason to do anything other than be governor for the next four years."

She was 10 years old when her father, a Baptist preacher and radio host, first ran for governor of Arkansas and lost, later winning two terms.

When he ran for the Republican presidential nomination in 2008, she worked as his national political director. Eight years later, she managed his second presidential bid. After a stint as a commentator on Fox News, she became the White House press secretary for Trump.

She shares her father's hard-edged conservatism and his taste for political combat.

The midterms were a "tough night for Republicans," she acknowledged, with the economy "the biggest driver" behind the results. "Any time you're going into a midterm and people are feeling that pressure, they tend to go against the party that's in power." Now, she said, Republicans should "draw a very distinct difference" with Democrats on economic and other issues.

"I think a lot of the people in some of those states are going to have buyer's remorse" about their new Democratic leaders, she predicted, "and we'll see a shift come back in '28."

Speaking of 2028, she also called Vance "certainly the frontrunner for the Republican nomination."

There is no shortage of sons who have followed their fathers into governorships − among them the Sununus of New Hampshire, the Cuomos of New York, the Chafees of Rhode Island, the Beshears of Kentucky .

But Sanders is the first and so far only daughter to be elected governor of the same state as her father. (Kathleen Sebelius, daughter of Ohio Gov. John Gilligan, was twice elected governor of her adopted state of Kansas.)

Being the youngest governor in the country (a data point Sanders repeats nine times in her book) means she would be just 46 at the next presidential election, in 2028, and only 50 at the one after that, in 2032. That would be two years after her second term ends, with Arkansas term limits preventing a third.

She will be first Democrat elected to lead Georgia since 1998. articles.title: House Republicans divided over how to move forward after brutal election losses
articles.summary: House Republicans are divided over how to move forward after the party’s devastating election losses, with some calling for an overhaul of the current leadership team and others arguing that President Trump bears much of the blame. Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) told staff on a call Wednesday that he would not run for minority leader,…
articles.body:
House Republicans are divided over how to move forward after the party’s devastating election losses, with some calling for an overhaul of the current leadership team and others arguing that President Trump bears much of the blame.

Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) told staff on a call Wednesday that he would not run for minority leader, setting the stage for a potentially bruising contest between House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) and House Judiciary Committee Chair Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) for the top post.

Meanwhile, House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) and House GOP conference Chair Lisa McClain (R-Mich.) are seeking to retain their leadership positions as the party transitions to the minority.

But Emmer faces a challenge from Republican Study Committee Chair August Pfluger (R-Texas), while Reps. Erin Houchin (R-Ind.) and Greg Steube (R-Fla.) are challenging McClain.

House Republicans are looking to sharpen their messaging strategy, effectively counter the Democrats’ agenda and position the party to win back the majority in 2028. Some conservatives say that will require new leaders to chart the path forward, rather than the old guard.

“I think if we send up the same leadership team that led us to the slaughter, we will look like clowns,” a GOP lawmaker, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, told The Hill. “You know, I mean, so you have to make change. Does that mean they all have to change? I’m not saying that. But you can’t have the same team.”

The lawmaker argued that GOP leaders failed to effectively communicate the party’s accomplishments and painted an overly optimistic picture of how Republicans would perform in the midterms.

“I think voters are upset. They expected us to go and fight for them, and then they saw us work on things like name, image, and likeness, or you know, or cryptocurrency reform, or whatever stuff that had nothing to do with making their lives better, and voters concluded we just didn’t care about them,” the lawmaker said.

A second GOP lawmaker echoed those sentiments, arguing the current leadership team didn’t take up bills he thought were important and veered away from conservative values to appease other factions of the conference, including moderates.

“We need all new leadership, top to bottom,” the lawmaker said. “And I’ve talked to several members that have said they will not vote for anybody else, anybody currently in leadership.”

Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (R-Fla.) took aim at the House GOP leadership team in a post on the social platform X , accusing it of fighting her efforts to advance a ban on stock trading, permanently prohibit the creation of a central bank digital currency and reform the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act.

Jordan, co-founder of the far-right House Freedom Caucus, has emerged as a favorite among some House Republicans.

“I think we’re going into a wartime situation where we are going to be the rebel alliance, and we’re going to need someone who knows how to fight, and Jim Jordan knows how to do that,” the first GOP lawmaker said.

But other Republicans argue that Scalise is better positioned to take the top spot, given his current leadership role. Scalise initially won the Republican nomination to be Speaker in 2023, beating Jordan in a secret ballot vote. But he withdrew from the race when it became clear he would not win enough support from his conference to get the votes needed on the House floor.

Jordan was later chosen as the nominee for Speaker, but he repeatedly fell short of the votes needed to secure the gavel.

“Steve is the right guy for the job. Plain and simple. He’s a tried and tested leader, who has the experience to lead House Republicans for the next two years, and the chops to reclaim the majority in 2028,” a third GOP member, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said.

“I think for Scalise … it’d be an easy transition for him to step into that. But for Jordan, he’s really — how do I phrase this? He’s been a loyal soldier. He’s rallied people well, and he’s an effective politician. So I think both would do well in the role, but I think Scalise would have an easier transition just out of pure — his House leadership currently,” a GOP staffer told The Hill last month.

Republicans are also split over the races for minority whip and GOP conference chair, with some backing incumbents Emmer and McClain, respectively, while others are throwing their support behind the challengers.

“I think Pfluger has done an excellent job as RSC chair, but to his credit, Emmer at least is a warrior. He’s a fighter. He’s a battler, and that’s what we’re going to need. So you know that’s a tough call,” the first GOP lawmaker said.

A fourth GOP lawmaker said the blame for a seismic election loss shouldn’t go to current House leaders but to the president.

“I mean, this is all on the president, and this war, and so the reason this, I mean, this blue tsunami happened and wiped out the Republican Party is because Trump wanted to protect his child rapist friends in the Epstein files, and then started a war with Iran, and that is why we’re in this situation. So I blame the man at the top. I don’t blame leadership,” the lawmaker said.

“I don’t think Mike Johnson actually deserves a lot of criticism, and then you know you’ve got Scalise and Emmer running, as what I’ve been told. I mean, they were the same guys that had been there. I don’t have a problem with that. … I don’t blame them at all. They were dealt a really s—ty hand,” the lawmaker said.

Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.), a centrist who is retiring at the end of his term, characterized the 2026 midterms as a “referendum on President Trump,” adding that candidates vying to be GOP leader would be as pro-Trump as Johnson was, regardless of who’s chosen.

“If you show me somebody that would push back a little bit and say, ‘Hey, Republicans have always been the party of free markets and free trade. Why are we going back on that? Why are we treating our allies bad?’ But all we saw was people accommodating the president’s worst instincts,” Bacon said Tuesday. “And so somebody who says that … we [should] have a new leader. OK, what would you have done differently over the last two years, and push back on some of this stuff? I hear from a lot of swing voters that they wanted Congress to be a check and balance to the worst, you know, egregious things that Trump does, but they didn’t see it.”

Trump told reporters on Wednesday that he would “stay out of” the race to pick a new House Republican leader after Johnson said he wouldn’t run.

Lisa McClain (R-Mich.), chair of the House Republican Conference; Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.); and Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.), meets with reporters ahead of a key procedural vote to end the partial government shutdown, at the Capitol in Washington, Feb. 3, 2026.

articles.title: GOP’s lame-duck plans unravel after election drubbing
articles.summary: Republicans’ hopes of finishing a big chunk of President Trump’s agenda in the lame-duck session of Congress are rapidly deflating in the wake of the blowout losses their party suffered in Tuesday’s election, according to Republican aides on Capitol Hill. Senate Republican sources say the bold talk before Election Day of ramming a budget reconciliation…
articles.body:
Republicans’ hopes of finishing a big chunk of President Trump’s agenda in the lame-duck session of Congress are rapidly deflating in the wake of the blowout losses their party suffered in Tuesday’s election, according to Republican aides on Capitol Hill.

Senate Republican sources say the bold talk before Election Day of ramming a budget reconciliation package through Congress to fund the Pentagon and the Iran war by circumventing a Democratic filibuster now seems unlikely after GOP candidates lost handily even in red states such as Texas, South Carolina and Kansas.

Vice President Vance has blamed the unpopularity of the war with Iran as the main reason for the GOP losses across the country, and Senate Republican sources acknowledge the conflict was a major drag on their party.

There’s a growing expectation among both Senate Republicans and Democrats that the annual funding bills, including money for the Defense Department, will get punted into 2027.

There’s rising concern that Congress’s 65-year streak of passing the National Defense Authorization Act is also in jeopardy.

Senate Republican sources are questioning whether permitting-reform legislation , which is scheduled to come to the floor next week, or the farm bill, a top priority of Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.), has any chance of passing Congress before Christmas now that Democrats are looking forward to big majorities in the Senate and House in January.

One senior GOP aide said the “logistics” of passing a budget resolution and a follow-up reconciliation package to fund the Pentagon and Trump’s emergency request for supplemental defense funding “is going to be difficult.”

“I don’t know if there’s an appetite there,” the source said, warning the annual defense authorization bill also faces an uphill climb.

Republican aides say that even if Thune and Senate Budget Committee Chair Ron Johnson (R-Wis.) are able to coalesce 50 Republican votes behind a budget reconciliation plan to fund defense priorities, it would consume weeks of floor time and face uncertain prospects in the House.

“I think the House is going to have some attendance problems, getting members back,” said a second senior GOP aide.

The source said there are strong doubts on the Senate side that House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) will be able to persuade all of his Republican colleagues to return to Washington for a six-week legislative sprint to finish Trump’s agenda after they got shellacked in Tuesday’s election.

House Republicans currently have a 218-seat majority, meaning it would take only a few absences to derail a budget reconciliation package, which wouldn’t receive votes from any Democrats.

Republicans fear that permitting-reform legislation, which appeared to have strong momentum at the end of September, may now also be in jeopardy after Democrats exceeded expectations by picking up at least seven Senate seats and at least 39 House seats.

One Republican aide on Thursday said “I’ll be surprised” if permitting reform passes.

The source pointed to comments Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) made on Wednesday questioning whether a final deal would be reached amid strong opposition to the bill from environmental groups.

Schumer appeared less bullish about the bill’s prospects than two key Democratic senators — Sens. Martin Heinrich (N.M.) and Sheldon Whitehouse (R.I.) — sounded when Congress left town weeks ago for the preelection recess.

Asked about the permitting-reform bill that Senate Republican leaders want to pass in the lame-duck session, Schumer would only say he “hoped” the bipartisan working group would reach a final deal.

“We have a bipartisan group working on permitting reform, and hopefully they’ll come up” with a deal, he said.

A second GOP aide on Thursday said Schumer’s comments appeared to walk back Democratic enthusiasm for the legislation that the two lead Democratic negotiators, Heinrich and Whitehouse, touted as a major accomplishment just a few weeks ago.

“Whitehouse and Heinrich said there was a deal,” the aide said. Whitehouse is the ranking member on the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, and Heinrich serves as ranking member of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee.

Senate Republicans had warned in September there was a danger that Democratic support for the emerging compromise would evaporate if floor action on the measure was delayed until after the election.

Frustrated Republicans say that if Democrats walk away from the legislation it would be a shame because it could delay an eventual deal on permitting reform for months — or longer — in the next Congress, if it even happens.

Republican and Democratic aides are more pessimistic about getting a deal on a year-end omnibus appropriations package to fund the government through fiscal 2027 in the next few weeks.

Government funding is due to expire on Dec. 11, and Democrats say the Senate Appropriations Committee is well behind schedule, as the committee’s chair, Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), who was defeated by Democratic challenger Troy Jackson in Tuesday’s election, hasn’t yet released any drafts of the Republican appropriations bills.

Democrats say that Trump’s insistence on spending a total of $1.5 trillion on defense while hardly increasing funding for nondefense social programs had effectively derailed this year’s appropriations process.

Democratic and Republican sources say it would be very difficult to put together a broader deal on the annual appropriations bills in the next few weeks with Trump agreeing to give Democrats major concessions.

The growing consensus among Senate Democratic and Republican sources is that Congress will be forced to pass another short-term government funding measure to keep federal departments and agencies operating through March.

That would give the new Democratic Senate and House majorities time to put together their own appropriations bills in time for floor votes in late March or April.

“I would anticipate a CR,” said a senior GOP aide, referring to a short-term continuing resolution to fund the government until late March or mid-April.

The aide said Collins and other Republicans on the Appropriations Committee would like to pass an emergency supplemental appropriations package attached to the stopgap funding measure, but they don’t know if Democrats will agree to that.

“I think there’s going to be a desire to do some sort of an appropriations,” the source said. “I think Collins has a real desire to get it done at this point of time. I foresee a CR until March.”

Democrats are signaling that Republican leaders would have to agree to a very good deal if any package of regular year-long appropriations bills is to pass before Jan. 1.

Senate Republicans are also working on a package of Trump nominees to confirm before they lose control of the upper chamber. But even that will consume valuable floor time as it will require Republicans to first pass a resolution to set up the floor procedure and then a follow-up vote on the package itself.
