articles.title: Vance takes GOP hits as DeSantis, Cruz emerge as early GOP winners for 2028
articles.summary: The fight for the 2028 Republican primary is beginning to take shape on the heels of the GOP’s devastating midterm losses, with Vice President Vance facing criticism for blaming the losses on the Iran war and other big-name Republicans appearing to stake out their own positions. The losses have created a huge opening for GOP White…
articles.body:
The fight for the 2028 Republican primary is beginning to take shape on the heels of the GOP’s devastating midterm losses, with Vice President Vance facing criticism for blaming the losses on the Iran war and other big-name Republicans appearing to stake out their own positions.

The losses have created a huge opening for GOP White House hopefuls, including Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and Sen. Ted Cruz (Texas), to go against Vance.

It’s a fact seemingly recognized by Vance, who was quick to blame the Iran war for the historic drubbings, and Republicans at large.

“The election results were bad news for every leader across the party, given the scale of the losses, but they were particularly tough for Vance’s 2028 prospects,” said Kevin Madden, the veteran Republican strategist who served as a senior adviser on Mitt Romney’s 2012 presidential campaign.

“Vance is now in the position of serving as a loyal vice president to a lame-duck president whose approval rating is in the 30’s and whose influence on the future of the party could be in question,” Madden added.

Vance has long been seen as the front-runner to succeed President Trump as the GOP standard-bearer. A close second has been Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

But questions are now being raised by Republicans over whether a candidate not directly tied to the administration would be stronger.

“Tuesday made clear that the stink on Vice President Vance and Secretary [Marco] Rubio may be too much to overcome as the election was a referendum on the job they are doing,” said one top GOP operative who has spoken to DeSantis.

“This certainly creates a lane for DeSantis, Cruz and others if they are willing to run in a potentially impossible year to win,” the operative added.

In blaming the losses on Iran, Vance put some daylight between himself and his boss. Trump, for his part, has doubled down in insisting his administration made the right decision to start the war.

“Vance’s profile as a candidate is directly tied to the Trump legacy. A candidate for 2028 without an ability to craft a more unique, independent profile of their own will face challenges in this next two-year cycle,” Madden predicted.

The GOP operative who spoke to The Hill said 2028 “is going to be a difficult year for Republican presidential contenders if there aren’t substantial changes.”

If there aren’t changes, the operative said DeSantis might wait until 2032 to run for president.

DeSantis over the last 48 hours or so has certainly sounded like someone with the White House on his mind.

The Florida governor, who unsuccessfully challenged Trump for the Republican nomination in 2024, was among the first this week to offer his own pointed view on what went wrong for GOP candidates, pointing to the war in Iran and high gas prices.

In an interview with SiriusXM host Stephen A. Smith, he accused some in his party of “gaslighting” voters by not acknowledging their economic anxiety.

DeSantis has also pointed out that the red wall in Florida, where the GOP won a Senate race and a gubernatorial contest, held. That’s an argument that would seem to point toward his leadership of the state.

Republicans did lose three House races in districts that were redrawn to give GOP candidates an edge, and they are behind in a fourth. The gubernatorial and Senate races were also closer than expected. But DeSantis can certainly make an argument about his state being a GOP bastion.

Cruz ahead of the elections had been more transparent about his ambition to run for president, saying he would entertain the idea of a 2028 run after the midterms.

On his podcast, Cruz compared the losses to the drubbing Republicans took after Watergate, a comparison that would seem to at least raise the issue of corruption as being a factor in the GOP’s terrible night.

He also criticized the Trump tariffs and the Iran war for raising costs.

“Food is too high. Gas is too high. Diesel is too high. Insurance is too high. Life is too high,” he said.

GOP strategists predict that after Tuesday’s results, their primary will be wide open.

“Vance is completely unacceptable to any Republican who can accurately assess the reasons for the pasting we received on Tuesday,” one former Trump campaign aide said. “It not only opens the door for others, it should soundly shut the door for JD Vance.”

Other Republicans say Tuesday’s results force Vance to stake his claim early or face the consequences of a more crowded field.

“Vance needs to announce first with the president’s endorsement,” said Susan Del Percio, the veteran Republican strategist. “If he doesn’t do it in January, it’ll look like a sign of weakness and everyone will know the president isn’t on board. And that’s the million dollar question: Is he out of favor with the president?”

One former Trump aide — who asked for anonymity to offer a candid assessment — said that right now, there’s “more space than less space” for other Republicans to enter the race.

“Let’s face it, Cruz and DeSantis were the winners in our party the other night,” the former aide said. “This is absolutely the beginning of the end of the Trump era.”

The former aide added that Trump “is still going to be a potent force in the primary. If he endorses you, that’s 30 percent right off the bat.”

But the former aide predicted it would be difficult for Vance to keep his distance from Trump and that he would be pigeonholed to his stances.

“Imagine, he’s going to have to answer to Trump’s whim or rant of the day every day,” the former aide said. “And he’s not going to stand in stark contrast to the president because Trump will shred him.

“That’s just not an enviable place,” the former aide added.

Since the elections, Vance has been under scrutiny from both Republicans and Democrats. Former White House press secretary Ari Fleischer, who served under former President George W. Bush, took to social platform X to counter Vance’s evaluation of the sweeping GOP losses.

“Please allow me to present a different perspective,” Fleischer said. “The problem was not the Iran War. It was the cease fire. If you start a war, you need to win it and finish it – otherwise don’t start it.”

Democrats also pounced on Vance’s remarks.

“For you to reduce it to a simple political calculation while we still have 50,000 troops in the Middle East, is one of the most crass, cynical things I’ve seen,” Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), wrote Wednesday on X. “You and President Trump got us into this war without a clear objective and without regard for the will of the American people. It’s cost us American lives and billions of dollars of American treasure with no end in sight.”

On Thursday, as political pundits were saying it was the end of the Trump era, Republicans said Vance’s political future remained murky at best.

“I think if you’re Vance you gotta take the nomination and pray you get someone on the other side like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez,” the first former Trump aide said, referring to the progressive representative from New York.

For now, Del Percio said, results aside, Vance “ultimately stands in the same place he did three weeks ago.”

“He only exists at the whim of the president,” she said. “And if Trump doesn’t endorse, will Vance go without the president’s endorsement? If he’s forced to do that, he will break with Trump and it will get ugly.”

articles.title: Gen Z men split from GOP in midterms, broke hard for Democrats
articles.summary: Tuesday was a big night for Democrats, and Generation Z was a big reason why. The voters were also a big part of the winning formula for the party in Texas, where some…
articles.body:
Tuesday was a big night for Democrats, and Generation Z was a big reason why.

Young voters aged 18-29 broke hard for Democrats, including young men, who had been an important constituency for President Trump in 2024.

The voters were also a big part of the winning formula for the party in Texas, where some of the biggest wins of the night were recorded.

Trump won 56 percent of Gen Z men in 2024, per AP VoteCast data. But in 2026, Democrats pulled them across the aisle.

Fifty-nine percent of white men aged 18-29 voted Democratic on Tuesday, according to an analysis from Tufts University’s Center for Information and Research on Civic Learning and Engagement (CIRCLE).

“The number one force driving young men to vote for Trump and Republicans in 2024 were promises about an improved economy. Most Americans, including Gen Z men, feel that the economy is now worse,” said Tyler Daniel, an assistant professor of political science at Roanoke University.

This doesn’t necessarily mean that young men have had a significant change in politics. It seems more like negative partisanship, or the concept of voting against, rather than for, a candidate or party.

Daniel, however, had expected them to sit out of the midterms. “This is an abnormal reaction from this age cohort when they feel disenfranchised by the political system,” he said.

Adam Pennings, executive director of Run Gen Z, an organization that recruits and mentors young conservative candidates, said the young voters who came to Trump in 2024 are the same ones who left in 2026.

“Gen Z is the cost of living generation, and they voted like it,” Pennings added. “A lot of Republicans didn’t realize how pessimistic young people were, specifically.”

The data shows it — the Harvard Youth Poll reported that only 9 percent of young adults said the country was headed in the right direction. For the first time in its history, the poll said that more respondents expected to be financially worse off than their parents, not better, at 27 percent and 25 percent, respectively.

While Democrats hammered messages on affordability, Republicans spoke of the culture war, which led young men to vote for the candidates who campaigned on lowering prices.

“Under the first Trump administration, the economy was better. Younger voters, especially younger men, may have been more likely to give Republicans a chance again in 2024,” said Melissa Deckman, CEO of the Public Religion Research Institute. While cultural issues were still relevant in the previous election, Gen Z men mostly voted by looking at their wallets.

“There’s a sense that the American dream is out of reach,” Deckman added.

Now, Democrats face pressure to deliver on their campaign promises.

“This is not a generation of folks who will acquiesce to transactional interactions. There’s a desire for candidates to show up with authenticity,” said Leela Strong, a director at CIRCLE.

Looking toward 2028, Daniel expects that the GOP will prepare to lead the America First movement that is currently splintering within the party. He pointed to podcasters Tucker Carlson and Nick Fuentes, both of whom are trying to capitalize on points that the MAGA movement originally made with Gen Z men.

“We will have to see whether or not MAGA can exist without Trump guiding politics,” Daniel said. “The Republican Party is going through a broader identity crisis, one that will only worsen once Trump leaves power in 2029, and it is too early to see where Gen Z men will fall into the mix.”

Gen Z made up 12 percent the midterm vote

Data from The New York Times found that 70 percent of voters aged 18-29 cast their ballots for Democrats, a 33-point shift from 2024.

The red-blue divide was striking in some reliably Republican states like Texas and Alabama, where 70 percent and 63 percent, respectively, backed Democratic candidates.

Only in South Dakota and West Virginia did a majority of Gen Z voters support the Republican candidate. And the margins were slim, with the GOP reaching just a 2-point and 3-point lead in South Dakota and West Virginia, respectively.

President Trump led former Vice President Kamala Harris by 30 points is South Dakota and 42 points in West Virginia among voters aged 18-29, according to exit polls.

Those figures were similar to the vote in the 2020 presidential election , where Trump led former President Biden by 18 points in South Dakota and 32 points in West Virginia.

Exit polling from The Associated Press found that across all generations, the economy remained voters’ top priority. But Gen Zers were most likely to say they cast their vote as a rejection of Trump, in line with earlier reporting that younger Americans were more likely to say they regretted voting for the current president.

Kimberly McGuire, the executive director at URGE, a reproductive justice organization that partnered with HIT Strategies for a national survey of young voters , said the cost of living drove Tuesday’s results and that neither party should take Gen Z for granted.

“I think there is so much to learn from this election about how Gen Z has really found their feet politically,” McGuire told The Hill. “Some of the things that are rising to the top are the way in which Gen Z voters should not be taken for granted and should be treated in many ways as a swing constituency.”

Going into Tuesday’s midterm elections, all eyes were on Texas.

State Rep. James Talarico (D) and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) were locked in a highly contested battle for Sen. John Cornyn’s (R-Texas) Senate seat, while State Rep. Gina Hinojosa (D) looked to unseat Gov. Greg Abbott (R).

Both races ultimately swung in the Democrats’ favor in historic wins for the party, and Democrats believe young voters played a huge role.

An exit poll from The New York Times found that 74 percent of people aged 18-29 voted for Talarico in this year’s Texas Senate race — a 49 point boost for Democrats compared to the 2024 election.

Kendall Scudder, chair of the Texas Democratic Party, noted that Gen Z “was a huge part of our coalition,” but there was no one group of Texans that drove Talarico’s and Hinojosa’s wins.

“What we did see consistently were people with low propensity, people who didn’t vote very often, maybe hadn’t voted before, showing up in much larger numbers than you would expect for a midterm,” Scudder said.

Texas has historically ranked 49th in the country for voter turnout, making it a big deal that younger generations flocked to the polls.

Talarico’s and Hinojosa’s campaign strategies to increase voter turnout targeted Gen Z, using tech-savvy, snappier techniques that Scudder believes worked in their favor.

“They weren’t necessarily just leaning on legacy media to get their messaging. You saw them running strong social media plans across different platforms, they had very functional TikToks, very functional Instagrams,” Scudder said. “It allowed them to reach people, get their message across and express the urgency — meeting people where they are.”

The Feed is a weekly scoop on Generation Z put together by three Generation Z editors at The Hill. We’re working to understand the ins and outs of our generation’s politics. Send tips or comments to awalker@thehill.com, jfeldstein@thehill.com or cleibowitz@thehill.com.

articles.title: Everyone called it a blue wave. But were the midterms more about independents?
articles.summary: In key races, independents flexed their muscle. But that doesn't mean they're turning Democrat.
articles.body:
The "blue wave" that decimated Republicans in the midterm elections is widely seen as the resurgence of the Democratic Party after its decisive defeat two years ago.

But there's more to the story than that.

"It wasn't just a blue wave. It was an independent voter tsunami," Jeremy Gruber, senior vice president at the nonprofit advocacy group Open Primaries, wrote in the aftermath of the vote.

Gruber believes the Democrats owe much of their victory to political independents, whose numbers eclipse those of registered Republicans and Democrats. "They are now America's kingmakers," he said in an interview.

Forty-five percent of Americans, a record high , identify as independents, up from 34% in 2002, and their muscle was seen in key races this week.

Per The Washington Post, "In Kansas, nearly 7 in 10 independents supported Democrat Adam Hamilton, while Texas Democrat James Talarico won nearly two-thirds of independent voters."

And NPR noted that Republicans fared poorly in part because GOP candidates didn't reach the threshold of the independent votes they needed to win. Early analysis shows that Republicans won 38% of independents; they needed 46% to do well, NPR said.

But the outcome of the midterms, which gives control of both the Senate and the House to Democrats, collides with Gallup research that shows just 43% of Americans have a favorable view of the Democratic Party. As PBS put it , "Swing voters don't really love Democrats, even if they voted for them."

Is it wrong, then, to consider what happened in the midterms a "blue wave"? And could those independent voters vote red again in another two years? The characteristics and motivations of independent voters provide a clue.

"A Democratic victory is not a Democratic mandate. Even after these results, roughly six in ten voters still have an unfavorable view of the Democratic Party. Independent voters did not suddenly become loyal Democrats," wrote Gruber, whose work at Open Primaries promotes primary elections that are open to everyone, regardless of party affiliation.

Findings from the AP Voter Poll of midterm voters were similar.

"Only about half of voters had a 'somewhat' or 'strongly' favorable view of the Democratic Party. That was higher than the approximately 4 in 10 who viewed the GOP positively, but not by much. About 2 in 10 voters who supported Democratic candidates had a negative view of the party as a whole," according to AP.

Many independents who voted for Democrats were actually voting against Republicans — and specifically, President Donald Trump who repeatedly said "pretend I'm on the ballot" throughout the campaign season — Gruber said in an interview.

"This was more than anything, a vote of rejection by independents, not a vote for the Democratic Party of its agenda," he said.

That said, when independents are asked whether they lean more to one political party than another, slightly more say they lean more to the Democratic Party.

And the two independents in the U.S. Senate, Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Angus King of Maine — caucus with the Democratic Party. (The one independent in the House, California Rep. Kevin Kiley, caucuses with the Republican Party, which he left in March after his district's lines were redrawn.)

According to Gallup polling in 2025, of the 45% of voters who identified as independents, 20% said they leaned Democratic, 15% said they leaned Republican, and 10% said they had no leaning.

But there is a wide variety among independents with respect to ideology, and they are found all over the political spectrum. And independent is not synonymous with moderate; many are moderate, one recent study found, but some are progressive or extremely conservative.

What they have in common is the sense that neither party represents them, said Yanna Krupnikov, professor of communication and media at the University of Michigan and the author of "Partisan Hostility and American Democracy," among other books.

"I think a big part of it may be a dislike of partisanship and, potentially, a dissatisfaction with politicians. If someone is dissatisfied with their party's leadership that does not mean that they agree with the other party's policies. Identifying as independent would feel better," Krupnikov said in an email.

Gruber said that there is disgust among independents with the vitriolic, "red-meat" approach to politics by both parties.

"All voters, but independent voters in particular, are looking for problem solvers, and they're willing to move outside of the party system to find those problem solvers. Unfortunately, they haven't quite found them," he said. That's why independent voters have shown the capacity for moving back and forth among the parties within a few years, he said.

That's clear in independents' support for Donald Trump over the past two years. Forty-three percent supported him during the 2024 campaign; that had fallen to about 25% in June of this year.

The change was particularly striking among Latino voters, 53 percent of whom identify as independent. The Latino embrace of the GOP in 2024 turned out to be temporary.

According to the Washington Post , "NBC News's exit poll found that they favored Democratic House candidates by 62 percent to 35 percent. A separate voter survey published by the New York Times showed Latinos backing Democrats by 69 percent to 30 percent, a 28-percentage-point shift in the partisan margin toward Democrats compared with the 2024 presidential election."

Last month, the actor Matthew McConaughey made a video that celebrated political independents and pushed back against stereotypes. "A true independent takes the best of both (parties). And that's not indecision. That's judgment," he said. He argued that that independents can be the most powerful lawmakers in Congress because they are the "majority makers," the people who decide the outcome of close votes.

Many saw the video as more evidence that McConaughey is preparing for a campaign of his own, possibly as an independent. He has touted the work of former West Virginia Sen. Joe Manchin, who with his daughter Heather Manchin founded the Independent Leadership Council to promote independent candidates for Congress .

But while independents showed their muscle at the ballot box this year, they did not perform well as candidates. There were 173 independents running for the House this fall and 50 for the Senate, according to tracking website The Candidate. No independent won.

But their increasing numbers and visibility make it likely that this will change, Gruber said.

And there is some evidence that the number of people who consider themselves independent is even larger than what Gallup reports.

When Open Primaries surveyed registered Democrats in New York City, the group found that 40% identified as independent; they had registered as Democrat in order to be able to vote in the primary, or stayed with the party out of lethargy or simply the comfort of a long-term affiliation, Gruber said.

The past decade has given rise to another category of voter: the politically homeless . Like some independents, those who describe themselves as politically homeless feel they have been excluded from the major parties; some want other options . But many independents are perfectly happy without a party affiliation; in fact, they prefer it, even without the sense of community that being active in a party can confer.

This is especially true for young adults, who came of age in a time of heightened partisan rancor: 56% of Gen Z identifies as independent, Gallup found, and 50 million of them were eligible to vote this year, according to an analysis by the Williams Institute at the UCLA School of Law.

"The two largest groups that voted Democrat in the midterms were people under 30, and Latinos. And those are the two largest contingencies of independent voters," Gruber said.

And the energy that these young voters and other independents brought to the midterms upended outdated stereotypes about independents, Gruber said: that "they're fence sitters, they're not involved, they don't care, they're disinterested."

"Independent voters showed up in huge numbers to say we absolutely do care, and we have something to say. In my opinion, this was the first real exhibition of the power of independent voters to decide a lot of races, and they did so."

Krupnikov, at the University of Michigan, noted that the outcome was an amalgamation of factors; it wasn't independents alone that gave Democrats the House and Senate.

"It is a combination of people's political choices, but it is also a question of turnout efforts.... And, Republicans are also important — both in the candidates they select and in their turnout decisions."

She added, "I am not sure we can put the responsibility on any particular group, rather so far the midterm seems like a collective moment where the preferences of many different groups happened to overlap in a really consequential way."

But as McConaughey said in his video, independents can sometimes be the deciding factor when votes are close, and Gruber said there is a clear message for both parties in the midterm results:

"You better start building bridges with independent voters because they are now America's kingmakers, and neither party has any type of long-term relationship with them."

Parties historically haven't liked independents because they can't control them, he said, and the parties' efforts to indoctrinate them or wish them away haven't worked. But they're going to have to forge a new relationship with independents going forward, he said, "because there are so many of them."

articles.title: One industry faces multitrillion-dollar reckoning after historic midterm election reshuffle
articles.summary: Donald Trump backed AI data centers, but Texas Democrats' historic midterm sweep now threatens billions in planned projects across the state.
articles.body: President Donald Trump has thrown the federal government's weight behind massive data center build-outs needed to power the country's artificial intelligence (AI) boom. But a historic Democratic sweep in Texas has put one of the nation's biggest AI infrastructure hubs under new political leadership, raising questions about the future of billions of dollars in planned investments. The victories marked a historic midterm night for Texas Democrats, who captured the governor's mansion for the first time in more than three decades and won a U.S. Senate seat for the first time since 1988. Texas is poised to overtake Virginia as the nation's largest data center market and is projected to account for roughly a quarter of new U.S. data center power capacity through 2030. With at least 248 projects planned across the state, investment bank Jefferies estimates that 13.3 gigawatts of announced developments could be at risk under a moratorium backed by Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa. ONE STATE IS GROUND ZERO AS TRUMP'S MULTIBILLION-DOLLAR TECH AMBITIONS FACE A MIDTERM TEST Texas was hardly alone in facing growing opposition to data center development. In Ohio, voters weighed 21 data center-related ballot questions across 18 communities in the midterm elections, more than any other state, highlighting the mounting resistance to America's rapidly expanding AI infrastructure. The results this week are now forcing some developers to reconsider where to invest billions of dollars in future projects as political power shifts. "It makes us and our investors pause and think if we should be investing somewhere else," Brittany Kaiser, CEO of Alpha Compute, told Fox News Digital following the Republican bloodbath in Tuesday's election. Kaiser warned that political shifts in traditionally Republican states could push billions of dollars in planned investments elsewhere, including overseas, as companies weigh growing opposition to data center development — especially within the Democratic Party. "There's new decision making that needs to come into play and a lot more to think about than there was before the election," she said. IT TOOK 3 MONTHS TO GET INSIDE THIS MASSIVE TEXAS DATA CENTER — HERE’S WHAT WE SAW But relocating projects already underway is far more complicated, particularly when developers have secured land, negotiated power agreements and committed substantial capital. "It's not very easy to pivot after you've already made contractual and financial commitments to these types of builds," Kaiser said. For projects still in the pipeline, however, companies have more flexibility. Kaiser said Alpha Compute has already invested in data centers in Canada, Europe and Mexico, where regulatory approvals are more straightforward. The backlash highlights growing tensions between Washington's push to accelerate AI development and voters' concerns about electricity costs and the impact of data centers on their communities. Kaiser urged incoming lawmakers to strike a balance between addressing community concerns and preserving what she called "the biggest economic opportunity of our generation." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "It's really important, yes, to make sure that data center companies are good actors and are doing things the right way," she said, calling for "common sense legislation and regulation" that allows developers to work with lawmakers and local communities. "If we can abide by those rules, then bans and moratoriums should not be the answer," Kaiser said. "It's just let's sensibly regulate and move forward in a way that is positively impactful for communities."

articles.title: Inside ICE's high-stakes raids targeting illegal migrants in NYC as chief rips sanctuary laws
articles.summary: Fox News Digital embedded with ICE agents as they tracked down and arrested two migrants, one of whom resisted in a tense street confrontation in Brooklyn.
articles.body: BROOKLYN, N.Y. — With New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani escalating his opposition to ICE, federal agents continue to carry out high-stakes street arrests that one of the agency's top officials says could be avoided if the city cooperated with federal authorities instead of enforcing its sanctuary policies. Fox News Digital embedded with ICE agents last Thursday, getting a rare, firsthand look at the surveillance, tense stakeouts and split-second decisions behind arrests on Brooklyn streets — while riding along with the agency's top local enforcement official as he blasted city and state leaders over policies he says put officers and the public at risk. The early-morning operation saw agents move in on two men, handcuffing them and rushing them into unmarked SUVs. The first arrest was over in seconds. The second turned into a tense struggle. MAMDANI CALLS ICE A 'ROGUE' AGENCY AFTER NYC SHOOTING, CLAIMS AGENTS VIEW LAW AS 'MERELY A SUGGESTION' Behind the wheel was Ken Genalo, head of ICE's Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) in New York City, who accused Mamdani, Gov. Kathy Hochul and the City Council of keeping dangerous offenders on the streets. "100% all of this is about politics. It is not about public safety," Genalo said as he sat in his vehicle while his team staked out a Georgian illegal migrant charged with sexual abuse. He argued that sanctuary laws force ICE to track down suspects who should have been handed over to agents at local jails. Instead, agents have to try and apprehend migrants on city streets. "They don't acknowledge the victims, they don't acknowledge the angel families, those that unfortunately have suffered severe loss due to illegal alien crime," he said. The operation came less than a week after Mamdani released a Spanish-language video advising New Yorkers on how to respond to ICE agents, as tensions flared following the shooting of a Dominican migrant who authorities say tried to ram officers with his vehicle. The migrant had been in the U.S. for just three years but had already racked up a lengthy rap sheet for theft, robbery, assault, drug and weapons offenses, according to DHS. The Brooklyn arrests came amid a wider enforcement push, with ICE arresting nearly 2,200 illegal migrants during a statewide crackdown in August, known as Operation Rotten Apple. But the ride-along with ICE revealed what those figures cannot: hours of painstaking surveillance, careful planning and tense waiting — all for arrests that can be over in seconds and quickly escalate. WATCH: NYC ICE official rips Mamdani, sanctuary laws after tense street arrests DHS BOSS REVEALS OVAL OFFICE PLAN TO 'WITHHOLD FUNDING' FROM SANCTUARY CITIES AFTER AGGRESSIVE NEW YORK BUST Inside ICE's predawn raids Before dawn Thursday, more than a dozen armed ICE agents gathered at a secret Brooklyn location, wearing protective vests marked "ERO." Commanders briefed them on several targets and the potential risks: one might be armed, another was an amateur boxer. The stark warnings offered a glimpse into the dangers agents face as they head onto the streets to carry out arrests. Agents checked their gear, attached body cameras to their vests and hit the streets around 5:50 a.m. Genalo drove an unmarked SUV, monitoring radio chatter and explaining how agents tracked their targets, what could go wrong and why timing was critical. The first target was Nika Tkeshelashvili, 40, a Georgian national who ICE said entered the United States illegally through the southern border in January 2023 and was arrested in September on a first-degree sexual abuse charge. The charge remains pending. His next immigration court hearing wasn't until October 2028 — a five-year wait that drew disbelief from Genalo. As the SUV rolled through Brooklyn, Genalo explained how agents establish a "pattern of life" — studying a suspect's routine to determine when and where to make an arrest. In Tkeshelashvili's case, the intelligence was surprisingly mundane. Agents believed he regularly emerged between 7 a.m. and 7:30 a.m. to move his car and avoid a parking ticket. Unmarked ICE vehicles took up positions along nearby streets while Fox News Digital waited with Genalo roughly half a block away, with a clear view of the apartment building where the Georgian national was expected to emerge. But as the minutes ticked by, he was nowhere to be seen. Genalo remained unfazed. Meanwhile, daylight crept across the neighborhood, bringing commuters, schoolchildren and growing traffic. Genalo explained that darkness was an ally during these operations, but as the streets filled, a discreet arrest became harder. MAMDANI DEMANDS TRUMP RELEASE ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT SHOT BY ICE AGENT AS PROTESTS ERUPT IN THE BRONX Even weeks of surveillance could not guarantee Tkeshelashvili would appear, Genalo explained. If he stayed inside, agents might have to return another day. Then, at 7:57 a.m., a voice broke over the radio. "Target one just stepped out with a cigarette going towards the car if I'm not mistaken," an agent reported. Genalo raised his hand and pointed toward the radio. "I think that's ours," he said as more chatter crackled through the SUV. "He's wearing a black vest, red shirt, red hat," another agent radioed. "Team two, that's Tango. That's Tango," an agent called out. Within moments, agents converged on Tkeshelashvili in the middle of the street. Genalo accelerated toward the scene, the arrest unfolding through the SUV's windshield. By the time Fox News Digital pulled up, officers had already handcuffed Tkeshelashvili and were moving him into a waiting vehicle. He remained calm and said little. Within moments, the team was moving on toward Target 2. Genalo hailed the arrest as "textbook" and "flawless," praising the intelligence, timing and surprise that allowed agents to secure their target without a struggle. Speed, he explained, was critical. Minutes earlier, we heard over Genalo’s radio that another ICE team had encountered agitators blowing whistles, shouting and warning locals that federal agents were nearby. The team was pursuing an Ecuadorian migrant who faced sexual misconduct charges involving a child, Genalo said, but the agitators disrupted the operation. "Why would you protest that we're trying to arrest this individual?" Genalo said. A tense struggle on Brooklyn streets As we pulled away from the first arrest scene, Genalo briefed us on the next target: Yves Frantz Augustine, 45, a Haitian national who ICE said entered the U.S. legally in 1997 but overstayed his visa. Ordered deported in 2006, he remained in the country, later amassing a criminal record that included an assault conviction for which he served seven years in prison, along with weapons offenses and a terroristic threat case, according to ICE. Augustine previously served seven years in prison for assault, but ICE's attempt to deport him in 2011 during the Obama administration failed because Haiti would not issue the necessary travel documents, Genalo said. ICE tried to take him into custody after further arrests, but New York authorities refused to hand him over despite three detainer requests, according to Genalo. Agents faced a major concern during this operation: Augustine was taking a child to school. Genalo explained that agents would wait until Augustine drops off the child before moving in, saying ICE policy is to avoid making arrests near schools or in the presence of children. Another team of agents was tracking Augustine from cars and on foot, relaying updates over the radio as Brooklyn's morning rush gathered pace. Genalo pulled up alongside the curb, explaining that Augustine was expected to walk straight toward our SUV. We waited as traffic rolled past and officers closed in on his position. At approximately 8:26 a.m., the go-ahead came over the radio. Agents quickly surrounded Augustine just ahead of our SUV, grabbing his arms as they tried to handcuff him. "Don't move! Police! Let me see your hands!" an officer shouted, drawing his weapon. "We have a warrant for your arrest!" another announced. But Augustine refused to put his hands behind his back, prompting the agents to press him against the metal shutters of a closed storefront as they struggled to cuff him. "No, no, no, no," Augustine shouted. "Sir, don't fight," an officer warned, while a third appeared and tried to calm him. "Just put your hands behind your back, sir," the third agent said, placing his hand on his shoulder. As agents led Augustine away in handcuffs, his jacket slipped down, revealing the words "it's all a trap" emblazoned across the back of his shirt. The front read "NOCOMP." He continued pulling back as agents moved him toward a waiting SUV, pleading for his children. "Think about my kids," he cried out, according to footage recorded by Fox News Digital. Appearing stunned, he continued questioning the arrest. "A warrant for what?" he shouted and asked to call his wife before claiming he was now a U.S. citizen. An officer showed him the warrant and gave him time to read it before placing him in the SUV. Genalo disputed the citizenship claim, citing Augustine's 2006 deportation order. The arrest took roughly four minutes, far longer than the first, before agents secured Augustine and cleared the street. Back in the SUV, Genalo said Augustine's resistance forced officers to use additional restraint techniques, explaining that agents typically move detainees to a secure location before transferring them to an ICE processing facility. "We want to get in, make the arrest, and get out as fast as possible," Genalo said. He also rejected accusations that ICE agents abduct or disappear people, defending the speed of the arrests as a safety precaution. "We don't kidnap people, we don't disappear people. We arrest people," he said. ICE vs. City Hall For Genalo, the arrests reflected a wider battle over law and order — with ICE trying to remove dangerous offenders while city leaders refuse to cooperate and protesters work to disrupt operations. "You have murderers on the street. I mean, that by itself is absolutely amazing that you can say you're keeping the community safe by releasing murderers back on the streets," he said. Genalo said both Brooklyn suspects had previously been in local custody, but authorities ignored ICE requests to hand them over. The refusals, he argued, wasted taxpayer money and put officers, suspects and the public at risk. During the stakeout for Tkeshelashvili, agents feared their cover was blown when an NYPD patrol car appeared, adding another hurdle amid limited cooperation with local police. Genalo suggested a resident may have called police, but the concern was quickly resolved. Genalo laid much of the blame on Mamdani, Hochul and the City Council, accusing them of putting political ideology ahead of public safety while allowing offenders to return to the communities they claim to protect. "They're criminals that committed heinous crimes. And they should not be in the community," Genalo said of many of the migrants ICE has been apprehending. For Genalo, a Brooklyn native and 34-year law enforcement veteran deployed to Ground Zero with a special response team after 9/11, the breakdown in cooperation is personal. He recalled when ICE worked closely with local police and had its own unit at Rikers Island, taking more than 100 people a week into custody directly from the jail. Today there is no cooperation. Genalo blamed former Mayor Bill de Blasio for ending the arrangement and said former Mayor Eric Adams tried to restore cooperation but was hamstrung by the City Council. Mamdani, meanwhile, has called for ICE to be abolished and publicly opposed its enforcement operations. Genalo repeatedly fumed over New York City's sanctuary policies throughout the ride-along, challenging city leaders to put the issue on the ballot and let New Yorkers decide whether police should cooperate with ICE. "Let the residents decide," he said. A bipartisan push for a public vote in 2024 and 2025 went nowhere. Genalo suggested council members feared the result. Genalo also criticized anti-ICE protest networks that monitor federal vehicles, alert residents and mobilize protesters when officers are spotted. articles.body:
Rep. Ayanna Pressley, D-Mass., is pressing her party to wield their power to push far-left policies such as passing Medicare for All and reparations, and abolishing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

During remarks on Tuesday, Pressley declared, "Alright, now as I close I have a message for my colleagues in the House who are likely watching. Democrats , when we have the power, you have to use it. Democrats, can you hear me now? When we have the power we have to use it.

"Now, please don't tell me about a majority, show me a majority. Show me a people-powered majority with a mandate for justice, with a mandate for compassion, with a mandate for progress," she declared .

"Democrats, don't just talk about healthcare justice, pass Medicare for All. Democrats, don't just talk about abortion justice, pass the EACH Act, and repeal the Hyde Amendment. Democrats, don't just talk about black lives mattering, enact reparations now. Democrats, don't just talk about ending ICE's terror, take every last dollar from them and abolish ICE," the congresswoman continued.

Pressley, a member of the progressive cadre of House Democrats known as " The Squad ," has served in the chamber since early 2019.

Republicans suffered an electoral rout during the midterm elections, resulting in the loss of the House and Senate majorities, though President Donald Trump can veto any legislation the Democratic-controlled Congress sends to his desk during his final two years.

"The fascist occupant of the White House tried his hardest to end DEI and has pushed Black women out of the workforce. Now, Black women are flexing their power and poised to lead at every level of government. And we're bringing friends," Pressley said Wednesday on X .

In a statement provided to Fox News Digital on Friday, White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster said, "President Trump promised to end divisive, racist policies and restore merit and efficiency. DEI ran rampant during the Biden Administration, and Americans ultimately paid the price for these destructive policies with a restricted labor pool, higher operational costs, and workforce inefficiencies. The Trump Administration will always promote equal treatment under the law for every American, regardless of race or ethnicity."

The Republican National Committee did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment on Friday.

articles.summary: Senior Republican lawmakers and strategists have reportedly pressed the Trump administration to fire the Pentagon chief and swiftly end the Iran war.
articles.body:
The White House faced calls for policy and personnel shakeups after brutal midterm elections, with the defense secretary under most pressure. Senior Republican lawmakers and strategists have reportedly pressed the Trump administration to fire the Pentagon chief and swiftly end the Iran war , blamed for fuel-price inflation that topped voters' concerns. Their calls add to mounting criticism of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

An outgoing Republican lawmaker will next week seek to begin impeachment proceedings in the House of Representatives, though it's unclear if such efforts will gain momentum in the Senate. US President Donald Trump's calculus on Hegseth is tricky: Firing him after the new Congress sits in January will require confirmation from a Democrat-controlled Senate.

articles.title: AI makes blackmail easier than ever. So how do you protect yourself?
articles.summary: It’s 2:30 a.m. and John writes into an app on his phone, “I don’t love my wife anymore. I’m just not attracted to her and I think I like my secretary Jenny.” No one else will see it. It’s just between him and AI. The app gently, kindly and with great understanding asks a follow…
articles.body:
It’s 2:30 a.m. and John writes into an app on his phone, “I don’t love my wife anymore. I’m just not attracted to her and I think I like my secretary Jenny.” No one else will see it. It’s just between him and AI.

The app gently, kindly and with great understanding asks a follow up question. When John opens the app in the morning and says “I changed my mind,” the app says, “No problem John. Your secret is safe with me.” But the next time John talks to the app in the middle of the night, it remembers everything and is just as understanding as before.

Millions of people now confide in AI (or rather in AI companions). It could be Google Gemini, Claude, Chat GPT, or one of the hundreds of apps that are actually marketed as AI companions and in many cases as AI girlfriends or boyfriends. Almost four years ago, I warned readers about an app called FaceApp that was taking images of your face in exchange for a silly filter. Three years ago , I warned that AI girlfriends were ruining an entire generation of young men. The trade is even more serious now, and it involves everyone.

People give these apps their inner lives, their most private thoughts, their most private medical issues and their most intimate relationships. That data is more valuable than we can possibly imagine.

As a data scientist, I can tell you why these conversations are just so rich with information. A search query into google is just a few words, but a late night confession, or a sensitive medical inquiry contains hundreds of words of context. It often specifies why the inquiry is being made. It illuminates exactly what users fear, whom they love, what they regret, their moods and their most intimate health issues. This is unlike anything data brokers have been selling for years and getting rich.

Most users assume their conversations disappear when they close their apps. It doesn’t.

In March 2023, a bug in OpenAI’s ChatGPT let users see the titles of other users’ chat histories. Payment information was exposed for more than 1 percent of ChatGPT plus subscribers. That was a bug, not a policy, but the point is, it was all there to be read … and used.

Employees are also a very serious security risk. You type your medical symptoms, divorce details or a workplace secret into one of these apps, and you’ve handed that text to a company, no matter what its privacy policy says. I have heard people say, well if you pay for the extra souped-up version, then the company doesn’t use your data to train their AI models and actually deletes it.

Please. What on earth have these tech companies done to gain our trust like this? We have case after case where they have manipulated , misinformed, and flat out lied to us about their actions. Just one example is when it came out that Amazon’s Alexa was not only listening to your family’s most private conversations in the home, but that without your knowledge, Amazon workers were also listening to those same conversations for “product development.”

And don’t even get me started on Meta’s manipulation of children or YouTube’s ad development for kids.

So even if you do look at the retention sections of the zillion page fine print terms and conditions, and you see where it retains the data for a certain period of time even if you delete the conversations and pay for the premium service, tell me one reason we should trust these tech companies.

And if you don’t pay? Well, then you should assume every single thing you say is available to the highest bidder. But pay or don’t pay, the company’s employees and contractors can review the messages for safety or quality. Service providers that host the data can access it. Chats can be produced in legal proceedings, and well any breach or hack — it’s all there for the taking.

I’m not arguing that these apps are useless. In fact, they are incredibly helpful, whether it be for work, medical questions, therapy or useless random questions that pop up at dinner. For a lonely person at 2 a.m., a responsive voice can probably be truly helpful. I have heard from many people that it can help keep them steady.

But there is no free lunch. Both help and surveillance can be happening in the exact same chat window. The trade-off is currently invisible to the user, and that is the biggest problem.

My best advice: First, decide what you should never type into that app (which is to say, anything you don’t want the entire world to know). Second, check the terms and conditions in the retention section, At least you can have some assurance there and turn off training anywhere you can. Third, if you want a conversation deleted, use the company’s deletion request process and save a copy of the confirmation. Will it completely protect you? No, but it’s better than nothing.

The column I wrote seven years ago asked a simple question, “Why do we give away so much so easily?” The answer then was vanity. The answer now is loneliness. That makes the stakes much higher. Companies have built products that feel like confidants, but they are anything but.

Dr. Liberty Vittert Capito is a Professor at Washington University in St. Louis, feature editor of the Harvard Data Science Review and the co-host of both Harvard’s and MIT’s data science podcasts.

articles.title: DeSantis comes out swinging as Vance takes heat
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ DeSantis makes his case ▪ Eisenkot piecing together coalition ▪ Colom expands lead in Mississippi ▪ Battle brews over House GOP leadership Tuesday was a bad night for many Republicans across the country. But not so much for Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R). The term-limited governor is seizing his political moment…
articles.body:
▪ Battle brews over House GOP leadership

Tuesday was a bad night for many Republicans across the country. But not so much for Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R).

The term-limited governor is seizing his political moment as Republicans in Washington — including potential 2028 rival Vice President Vance — reckon with the fallout from a midterm thumping, driven largely by the Iran war, which voters blame for high gas, diesel and grocery prices.

DeSantis got a post-election boost on Polymarket, where his odds of winning the 2028 GOP nomination increased from about 4 percent before returns came in to 12.7 percent by Thursday evening. Vance’s odds briefly fell below 30 percent on election night before rebounding to 37.8 percent on Thursday, within a percentage point of where he stood before the election.

DeSantis is using the opening to make a case for his own record, touting his state’s work on immigration and pointing to Florida as a state where Republicans held their ground on Tuesday.

“To call it a ‘wave’ I don’t think would be fully accurate,” DeSantis said at a news conference Wednesday. “It’s the political equivalent of a meteor strike that went all around the United States — blue states, red states, everything in between.”

The Florida governor said Republicans in his state managed to “hold the line” and maintain GOP control this year — even though Rep. Byron Donalds (R), the Sunshine State’s newly elected governor, was ahead by just 1.3 percentage points, far short of DeSantis’s 19.4-point reelection margin in 2022. Democrats also won a handful of House seats in Florida despite redrawn district lines meant to benefit Republicans.

“Of the 10 largest states in this Union, only one state will have Republican control of their state — the state of Florida,” DeSantis added.

DeSantis also took aim at former 2024 GOP presidential rival Vivek Ramaswamy, a Vance ally, saying Democrat Amy Acton “beat Vivek like a drum” in Ohio’s governor’s race Tuesday and questioning why Trump’s team pushed him to run in the first place.

“You know, Vivek, he’s a — like a tech guy, he did this Alzheimer’s drug, and he wants to bring in people, foreign worker on visas,” DeSantis said on Sage Steele ’s podcast Wednesday. “ That is not the type of person that’s going to sell.”

DeSantis was warning before the polls closed Tuesday that the war with Iran was hurting Republicans and argued the conflict contradicted the President Trump ‘s campaign pledge of keeping out of new wars.

“The Republican mantra since Trump came on the scene was that we don’t want to get into these open-ended conflicts, and that’s what this has become,” DeSantis said in a CNN interview this week. “A little bit different than Iraq, for sure, but I think this one was important because it had a direct effect on people’s pocketbooks.”

He also roasted Republicans for trying to blame high prices on former President Biden , rather than the war, saying, “When you gaslight people, they don’t trust you on anything else.”

DeSantis, who took on Trump in a bitter 2024 primary, has more room to criticize the administration than some of the other potential 2028 presidential contenders. He has spent nearly two years of Trump’s second term governing Florida, giving him distance from unpopular decisions made in Washington.

Vance, meanwhile, has a tougher balancing act. He blamed the GOP’s election losses on the Iran war and questioned the cost, but he stopped short of criticizing the decision to go to war itself.

If he decides to run for president in 2028, the vice president will have to answer for the administration’s record while trying to hold on to the coalition that helped elect Trump in 2024. That’s looking harder than ever.

The Hill’s Amie Parnes has a new look today at how the 2028 GOP primary is shaping up. While Vance has long been seen as the front-runner to succeed Trump, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio following as a close second, Parnes reports that Republicans are now asking questions about whether a candidate not directly tied to the administration would be stronger.

INCHING CLOSER : Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot appears to be closing in on becoming Israel’s next prime minister as 67 of the 120 incoming members of parliament have declared their support for him to replace Benjamin Netanyahu .

Eisenkot met with Israeli President Isaac Herzog on Thursday as Herzog weighs which party leader will have the first chance to form a governing coalition following Israel’s parliamentary elections last week. Herzog has been meeting with the leaders of all the parties throughout the week.

The president, who mostly holds a ceremonial role except for having the responsibility to choose someone to form a government after an election, said representatives from factions representing 67 lawmakers have recommended Eisenkot be chosen to form a government.

This came after the leaders of multiple parties, including two Arab groups, declared their support for Eisenkot.

Still, some hurdles remain. Some members of Eisenkot’s coalition had previously expressed opposition to forming a government with the Arab parties, and Herzog said he would work to clarify the situation before choosing someone to form a government Sunday.

If Eisenkot is chosen and is successful at forming a government, it would bring an end to Netanyahu’s administration. Netanyahu has served for the past four years since returning to the role following a brief stint out of power.

Mail-in ballots are allowed to be counted for up to five business days in Mississippi as long as they were postmarked by Election Day.

The Senate GOP’s campaign arm urged county election commissioners and circuit clerks Thursday to separate and preserve the provisional ballots from the rest, a move that Colom’s campaign denounced as a “desperate stunt.”

If Colom hangs on to win, it would be a shocking upset for Democrats to add to their sweeping victories.

GOP Reps. Erin Houchin (Ind.) and Greg Steube (Fla.) both intend to oppose McClain as the party considers its best path forward. Houchin announced her candidacy Wednesday in a letter to her colleagues, while a source familiar with the matter confirmed to The Hill’s Sudiksha Kochi on Thursday that Steube plans to run .

The developments come as Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) has indicated he doesn’t plan to run for minority leader, setting up a battle between House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) and House Judiciary Committee Chair Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) for the job.

On the other side of the aisle, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) seems all but certain to become the next Speaker. But one battle is brewing as Rep. Sean Casten (D-Ill.) is challenging Rep. Maxine Waters (D-Calif.) to lead the House Financial Services Committee.

Trump’s lawyers argued that Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg ‘s (D) legal theory behind the case was preempted by federal campaign finance law and that his team wrongly showed jurors official acts from Trump’s time in the White House, including online posts.

Bragg’s office maintains none of the evidence was protected. The Hill’s Zach Schonfeld reports the arguments left several judges questioning where to draw the line.

ON THE OUTS? Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth ‘s fate in the president’s Cabinet seems up in the air as critics point the finger at him for pushing Trump into a war with Iran that contributed to widespread losses in the midterms.

The Hill’s Filip Timotija and Julia Manchester report that two sources familiar with the discussion said Trump is asking allies about Hegseth’s standing. One of them said the Pentagon chief is in “a lot of trouble,” while the other said how much danger he was in isn’t clear.

One of the sources said the conversations are happening as the administration is reviewing plans to resume military action against Iran.

Trump defended Hegseth on Thursday, saying he has “every intention” of keeping Hegseth in the role, but he also acknowledged that replacing him would be easier to do before Democrats take control of the Senate next year.

Sources previously told The Hill that Hegseth has expressed interest in Sen. Marsha Blackburn ‘s (R-Tenn.) Senate seat now that she’s been elected governor of Tennessee. Trump said Wednesday that Hegseth would be “very popular” if chosen to replace her.

But a person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press that Hegseth isn’t currently being considered for the seat.

A senior Pentagon official told The Hill on Thursday that the idea of replacing Hegseth is not “practical” given the difficulty of finding a replacement who could be confirmed by the Senate during the lame-duck session.

Democrats are widely expected to pursue investigations into Hegseth in the next Congress. More immediately, Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) plans to introduce articles of impeachment against him next week.

CONVICTED : Actor Russell Brand was found guilty Thursday on charges of rape and sexual assault based on allegations from more than 20 years ago.

The verdict was rendered after a jury made up of eight men and four women deliberated for more than eight hours over the course of two days. The trial began just a little more than three weeks ago.

Brand was convicted on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault based on accusations from four women. He was found not guilty on two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

He’s set to be sentenced Monday, and Judge Joel Bennathan said Brand faces a “significant” prison term. Brand had been free on bail but was taken into custody after the verdict.

Allegations against Brand have been raised for years and received greater attention following reporting from British media a few years ago. He was first charged in spring 2025 following a police investigation.

Brand denied the allegations. He acknowledged being obsessed with sex when he was younger but said he would never have forced anyone against their will.

Brand had been a mainstream actor who appeared in major movies such as “Forgetting Sarah Marshall” and “Despicable Me” in the 2000s and 2010s. articles.title: Democrats, get to work lifting families with bipartisan fixes to childcare
articles.summary: Consolidating existing pro-family programs could win bipartisan appeal.
articles.body:
Victorious Democrats, rightly fearing the American family’s demise, must now deliver, from affordable day care and housing to heftier tax benefits. But what to do? How can they unite centrist Democrats and more left-leaning progressives to buoy parents and make child-rearing feasible once again?

Democratic candidates floated a variety of affordability fixes on the campaign trail. Now the real work begins, ideally in bipartisan fashion. Democratic leaders might even hold their noses and give Vice President JD Vance a call.

The progressive left pushes Scandinavian-style entitlements like free childcare, the marquee initiative pressed by New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani. He insists that the government must finance additional caregivers outside the home — starting when babies turn just six weeks old — so mom and dad can pursue careers or merely keep food on the table.

But it turns out that most parents prefer staying home after a newborn arrives, favoring paid family leave rather than stashing toddlers in daycare, as a survey of American families revealed last month. In addition, entitlements come with a huge price tag, projected at $9 billion in New York — while subsidizing affluent parents , along with employers who reap freed-up labor, letting taxpayers foot the childcare bill.

Vance arrives from a different angle, pressing a basic question that every parent asks: How can I spend more time with my young child, while earning enough to sustain my family? Then he stumbles, taking social engineering to a whole new level. Vance wants to capture federal aid currently helping employed lower-income parents pay for childcare, sending these dollars to well-off families — if one parent agrees to stay at home . The vice president would impose his own rendition of family onto all Americans.

Still, leading Democrats see the underlying policy quandary, which is whether the government should help parents better nurture kids at home, rather than only funding more childcare and pre-K outside the household.

Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), the vocal House member from Silicon Valley, has proposed $100 billion in new childcare spending each year, a package that would be “value neutral between staying at home, going to a childcare center, or having friends or family” provide daycare. This is consistent with the past half-century of detailing how parents contribute far more to a child’s early growth, or developmental delays, than do caregivers outside the home.

Another strategy could unite Democrats and newly minted moderate Republicans: Simplify the four tax credits and two federal programs that already finance childcare and preschools across the land. That is, make childcare affordable for more families by simplifying programs, rather than adding duplicative initiatives.

You may recall President Joe Biden’s expanded child tax credit , awarding families $3,600 for each child under 5 in 2021, a short-lived reform enjoyed by millions of middle-class families, while slicing the nation’s child poverty rate by half .

Vance pledged in 2024 to boost the Biden credit to $5,000 per child — a promise he has yet to keep. The vice president will certainly revive such pro-family ideas, remaking himself as kinder and gentler, tiptoeing toward the political center. And Vance remains relevant in moving bipartisan reforms through the White House.

Consolidating existing pro-family programs could win bipartisan appeal. On top of the child tax credit, Washington awards another three tax benefits — going to parents and employers — which help offset childcare expenses. This maze of programs costs the treasury about $201 billion annually in tax spending. It’s so confusing that just 1 in 7 parents even file for the child and dependent care credit.

Beyond funding thousands of Head Start preschools, the feds send a childcare block grant to the states, distributed to families as portable vouchers, allowing parents to pay grandma, even boyfriends in California, for their caregiving.

On top of this bevy of initiatives, 14 states and Washington, D.C. finance paid family leave for parents after a newborn arrives, commonly supported through payroll taxes that balance contributions from workers and employers.

Democratic socialists might recognize that their Scandinavian comrades embrace family leave as heartily as childcare. Parents in Norway benefit from 12 months of paid leave, split evenly between both parents. Finland offers a home allowance for stay-at-home parents — often fathers — until their youngster turns three years old, valuing the child’s robust growth over a parent’s quick return to work.

Ensuring the vibrant growth of young children is central to any society. Democrats can advance this essential project by simplifying access to myriad programs and investing in those that truly lift families. This blossoming of family supports just might spring from bipartisan soil, nourishing a newly productive Congress.

Bruce Fuller is an education and policy professor at Berkeley School of Education and the author of “Debating Childhood and Preschool.”

articles.title: Schumer vows Senate Democrats would block any ‘right-winger’ Trump Supreme Court nominee
articles.summary: Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) says Democrats would block any “right-winger” President Trump attempts to appoint to the Supreme Court after they take control of the Senate, which could ramp up pressure on conservative Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas to retire this year. “The bottom line is we’re not going to allow a…
articles.body:
Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) says Democrats would block any “right-winger” President Trump attempts to appoint to the Supreme Court after they take control of the Senate , which could ramp up pressure on conservative Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas to retire this year .

“The bottom line is we’re not going to allow a right-winger on the court,” Schumer told The Associated Press in an interview.

Schumer’s vow to oppose any Trump nominee to the Supreme Court in the mold of Alito, Thomas or the late Justice Antonin Scalia raises the prospect that there could be a vacancy on the court for many months if a justice retires or dies before Trump leaves office in January of 2029.

This could put pressure on Alito, who is 76, or Thomas, who is 78, to consider announcing their retirement from the high court in the next several weeks before Republicans lose control of the Senate.

Court watchers generally think Alito is more likely to step down next, though he has told friends he doesn’t plan to give up his job before the end of the year, according to The New York Times .

Schumer’s warning is not unexpected after former Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) kept Scalia’s seat vacant for nearly a year during the end of former President Obama’s second term.

The Senate eventually confirmed Justice Neil Gorsuch, a Trump nominee, in April of 2017 to replace Scalia, who died in February of 2016.

Schumer warned weeks before the midterm elections that Trump nominees would have a tough time getting confirmed in a Democratic-controlled Senate.

“If the nominees are as crappy as his present ones, very few of them are going to get through,” Schumer told Semafor .

“It’s the quality of the candidate that matters. Thus far, Trump has a record of notoriously bad candidates.”

Schumer told reporters Wednesday that Democrats aren’t putting a blanket hold on Trump’s judicial nominees but urged the president to advance judges and lawyers who are rated as well qualified or qualified by the American Bar Association (ABA) and have a demonstrated record of adhering to the law.

The ABA rated more than 200 of former President Biden’s judicial nominees, or about 85 percent, as well qualified, its highest rating.

“We want judicial nominees like we showed in ‘23 and ‘24, who obey the law, who have fidelity to the rule of law,” he said of the nominees Biden advanced to the Senate. “Too many of Trump’s nominees did not have that at all.”

articles.body:
[ Watch Whole Hog Politics Live : Hill Insider members can join us live today at 9 a.m. ET as Chris Stirewalt and host Bill Sammon go deep on this week’s political news. Members can join the discussion and pose their questions to Bill and Chris. Tune in! ]

In the long-running TV comedy 30 Rock, the protagonist, Liz Lemon , played by Tina Fey , has an on-again-off-again love interest in Dennis Duffy, played by Dean Winters (aka the mayhem guy from the insurance commercials).

The Duffy character has ended up having a surprising bit of political relevance, most notably for a 2008 episode that prefigured some of the changing nature of the Republican Party. Duffy is hailed as a hero for saving a commuter’s life on the subway, and the show’s preeminent Republican, Alec Baldwin ’s Jack Donaghy , tries to recruit Duffy as a candidate.

Duffy, a grifter and a fool, describes his ideological views as “fiscal liberal, social conservative.” In 2008, that was a laugh line, since in those days, many Republicans tired of the long battles of gay marriage and abortion had adopted the inverse — fiscally conservative, socially liberal — as a way to distance themselves from the long culture war that was alienating the party from many college-educated and upwardly mobile voters.

Indeed, the “new right” movement that would grow out of the defeats of the following eight years would be of a Dennis Duffy kind. President Trump and his MAGA movement weren’t conservative on those old issues, but it definitely embraced a kind of right-wing populism in which big government and big spending were paired with an enthusiastic form of culture war. It was a world in which Republicans shrugged off $2 trillion deficits and a sitting vice president would brag that Americans “do not have to apologize for being white” anymore — a world Duffy might have imagined.

But the Duffy-Lemon dynamic was actually a pretty good template for the tempestuous relationship between Trump and his adopted party. Duffy’s signature line after every breakup or encounter with Lemon was, “You’ll be back, dummy.” She would fume at his gall and her own weakness for falling for his old lines again, but he was right. And so was Trump . Every time it seemed like this time was the moment that the GOP had finally had enough, they came back again and again.

Trump has now led Republicans to what is already a worse midterm defeat than the 1974 Watergate-era catastrophe — and we’re still counting. With the potential loss of as many as 55 House seats, nine Senate seats and six governorships, 2026 may end up ranking with former President Herbert Hoover ’s 1930 rout on the list of worst-ever midterms.

There is a debate among Republicans only just now beginning over which factions of the party — the nationalists led by Vice President Vance or the mostly leaderless conservatives whose laments were expressed this week by Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) — are most to blame.

But it isn’t really that complicated. The midterms were about Trump and Trumpism, and because the GOP had so fully given itself over to him after his 2024 comeback, the damage left no corner of the party untouched.

Trump had in the past benefitted from resistance from factions within his party. But in the final iteration of MAGA, there was no creative tension and none of the “guardrails” we used to hear so much about. In his first term, friction with congressional leaders and governors helped keep some of Trump’s most damaging impulses in check. In the second Trump term, they refused him almost nothing — except for the abolishment of the Senate filibuster, which Republicans are about to rediscover as a principle pillar of the republic.

And it all ended in tears Tuesday, setting up a lame-duck period that promises to be an absolute grind for a party that would very much like to be able to turn the page on what will come to be remembered as a very embarrassing episode in its history.

Breaking up is hard to do, but it would appear that voters have done for Republicans what they couldn’t do for themselves.
