Mojo : “Early May, 1976. Deep in the Louisiana swamps, the musicians of Bob Dylan ’s Rolling Thunder Revue are spending the afternoon with Bobby Charles , the cult hero who’d made an album with The Band in 1972, and who also, in a previous life, had written See You Later, Alligator. On the road down South for the second Rolling Thunder tour, a show has been cancelled and Charles – whom Dylan later calls ‘one of the most melodious voices ever transmuted into a piece of vinyl’ — has invited everyone to his place in the bayou for a barbecue. But he isn’t cooking hamburgers. According to percussionist Gary Burk e, not long before his passing earlier this year, ‘There were a lot of local characters and this unusual-looking stew. I said, What is this? This guy with a Bowie knife in his belt, somebody you don’t want to mess with in a dark alley, says, ‘It’s alligator. I caught this last night.’’”

Levin: Voters are done with Trumpism : National Review: “ President Trump wanted voters to behave like he was on the ballot in the 2026 midterms, and he sure got his wish. Voters delivered a massive repudiation of Trump and Trumpism as they understand them, and the resulting wave washed away essentially every congressional Republican thought to occupy a competitive seat and many more besides. That’s not to say this presidency has entirely lacked for achievements. The Trump administration really seems to have gained control of the southern border, for instance, and has effectively pushed back on some of the excesses of Covid-era wokeism, both of which were (rightly) high priorities for many 2024 Trump voters. Some lower-profile but still important measures have advanced in some agencies, too. But these have been overwhelmed by the broader tenor of this administration, which has utterly lacked any public-spirited vision or direction and has allowed itself to be defined by Trump’s own vapid impulsivity and thuggish narcissism, and to descend into shameless personal corruption.

Trende: Biggest GOP flop since 1974: Poll Vault: “This was an absolute disaster for Republicans. There’s no mincing words, rationalizing, second-guessing, or beating around the bush: However bad you thought that last night could be for Republicans, it was worse. … Everything the Trump Administration did gave a sense of a governing class that was out of control. The UFC ring on the South Lawn. The White House ballroom. Changing the name of Lake Ontario. The ad hoc tariffs. From the point of view of a family struggling to make ends meet, Trump was offering them next to nothing, while giving off a sense that he was doing things simply to do them. … Good news for Republicans: Elections happen again. That’s the most important thing. I’ll probably write more on this later, but our constitutional structure wisely provides for another election in two years.”

Silver: GOP on a tightrope: Silver Bulletin : “[H]ow in the hell are Republicans going to go about picking an appealing candidate for 2028? [Vice President] JD Vance is the leader in prediction markets, but he’s Trump’s vice president. Marco Rubio , the other frontrunner, is the Secretary of State. I’m not sure there’s any John McCain looming on the horizon because it’s hard to be a McCain in Trump’s version of the Republican Party, which constantly excommunicates dissenters. So really my argument is this. It seems unlikely to me that Trump’s approval rating, currently 38 percent, is liable to get all that much better. The decline in his numbers over the past two years has been remarkably persistent, instead. Plus, he’s 80 years old, and doesn’t seem to care about the implications of his unpopularity for anyone else in the Republican Party. I don’t think anyone is expecting him to attempt a Clintonian pivot, much less to pull it off. And the Republican nominee in 2028 will have to navigate an incredibly treacherous tightrope: distancing themselves just enough from Trump without triggering his ire. This produced a massive fail for [Florida Gov.] Ron DeSantis last time around.”

Bob Crawford: Lessons from 1946: The Dispatch : “In the 1946 midterms, Republicans captured the national mood in two words: ‘Had Enough?’ Voters answered yes. Republicans secured 55 House seats and 12 Senate seats, winning both chambers for the first time since 1928—before the Great Depression and World War II. Eighty years later, ‘Had Enough?’ is being asked again, this time of a Republican president. … Today we remember midterm elections for their margins, but the deeper lesson is that these contests are harbingers of what may unfold in the next chapter in the American political story. Nobody in November 1946 thought they were electing two future presidents and the man who would give his name to an era of fear. They thought they were voting to lower the price of meat. That Republican majority lasted only two years. The people it brought to Washington shaped American politics for decades.”

Mod squad swamps the old squad : The New York Times : “For much of the midterm campaign, progressive Democratic insurgents commanded the spotlight in the fight to wrest control of Congress, defeating establishment incumbents in primaries, drawing enthusiastic crowds and promising to reorder their party’s priorities and remake American politics once they got to Washington. But the path to Democrats’ sweeping victory this week, when they seized control of both chambers of Congress, was paved overwhelmingly by moderates who had spent months persuading voters in Republican-leaning states and competitive congressional districts that they could be trusted to govern and would deliver dissatisfied voters a practical alternative to President Trump.”

Polls understate Democrats for a change: The Atlantic : “Heading into the midterms, everyone who follows American politics had the same question: Were the polls correct, or would they underestimate Republicans once again? The answer turned out to be neither. This time around, the polls undercounted a different kind of voter: Democrats. According to the Silver Bulletin polling averages, Democrats were on track to win the U.S. House popular vote by nine points and narrowly flip a few Senate seats in states that Donald Trump had won by double digits. … In fact, even this year’s seemingly incredible poll numbers turned out to significantly understate Democrats’ strength. Democrats are now expected to win the House popular vote by 13 points, the largest such victory in 50 years. And that four-point national polling error was small compared with the miss in certain states. In South Carolina, polls underestimated the Democratic candidate by five points on average; in Mississippi, by seven; in Texas, Georgia, and North Carolina, by nine.”

articles.title: Democrats’ big blue wave will destroy the economy
articles.summary: President Trump is right that the U.S. economy is the envy of the world. What a shame that Americans just voted to destroy it. That is not an exaggeration. Granting such a sweeping victory to the Democratic Party, now in thrall to progressives who want to hike taxes, abandon fossil fuels and shut down the…
articles.body:
President Trump is right that the U.S. economy is the envy of the world . What a shame that Americans just voted to destroy it.

That is not an exaggeration. Granting such a sweeping victory to the Democratic Party, now in thrall to progressives who want to hike taxes, abandon fossil fuels and shut down the rollout of artificial intelligence, will slow investment and neuter the industries powering U.S. economic growth.

Yes, voters are angry about the rising cost of living, blaming the war in Iran for higher oil prices. But restricting domestic oil and gas production, as Joe Biden did during his term and the environmental lobby is keen to do going forward, will not bring diesel prices down — just the opposite. The U.S. is the world’s largest oil producer ; limiting supplies in any global market inevitably drives prices up.

Similarly, banning the construction of data centers won’t make electricity cheaper; it will simply mean that fewer electricians and welders have work. The better answer lies in local regulations that protect residents from extra power and water costs resulting from data center operations.

There were some 45 ballot measures available to voters on Tuesday that restricted or regulated data centers; nearly all passed . Ohio, a major player in the space, led the country in seeking voter input. A local civics professor told Fortune that the response to the more than 100 referenda in the state should “signal to statehouses nationwide that ratepayer protections, transparency, and grid safeguards should dominate policy agendas.”

That would not satisfy U.S. Rep. Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.), who recently posted, “Top of the Democratic agenda on day 1 needs to be a pause on advanced AI development, regulation of this out of control industry, and a ban on artificial superintelligence.” No wonder tech stocks got hammered yesterday.

Throughout the 2026 campaign, Democratic candidates’ central promise was that they would deliver “affordability.” But the media — and voters — failed to demand specifics. Exactly how will they make life more affordable? There is no plan.

Democrats will not make anything cheaper, they will simply raise taxes and increase regulations. The costs of both will be passed on to consumers in the form of higher prices.

How do we know? Because that is what is already happening in Democrat-run cities and states, the most expensive places in the nation to live . Not only are these states prone to high taxes and regulatory gridlock, but they also host expanded and often unaffordable welfare programs meant to woo voters. There is no attention paid to increasing supply, which brings down prices — only to subsidizing higher demand.

Socialists want to go further than that traditional Democratic playbook, by inserting the government into private market activity. In New York City, for instance, Democrat Mayor Zohran Mamdani campaigned partly on a promise to lower food prices. He intends to build a handful of city-run grocery stores that will offer consumers discounted goods. Because the government is involved, the first store is estimated to cost $30 million — more than $3,000 per square foot and roughly four times the norm. The store is expected to run at a loss, forever.

There is nothing about this project that makes sense; it is a left-wing fantasy that will end in tears.

Democrats are offering up vague and unworkable promises, not real solutions. Roy Cooper (D), the new senator-elect from North Carolina, promises on his campaign website to “make stuff cost less.” James Talarico (D), elected to the Senate from Texas, wants to cap credit card rates , ignoring the long-failed history of price controls.

Some Democrats have vowed to eliminate tariffs. That is one step that could offer price relief, but it might also slow investment coming in from overseas. And Fed economists have determined that the impact will be slight.

Democrats seem eager, generally, to reshape the U.S. to resemble Europe, which cannot grow and offers its young people few opportunities. But the European Union has lost its mojo, more eager to divide the spoils of entrepreneurship and innovation than to encourage those hallmarks of American progress.

Government spending now accounts for nearly half of the EU economy , compared to about 35 percent in the U.S. Governments there have adopted “socialist-light” policies that guarantee slower productivity growth and a creep toward the gray twilight of mediocrity.

European countries have expanded their welfare states at the expense of their industries and their national defense, all but inviting Russia to invade Ukraine and threaten its NATO members. The proud automobile companies of Germany are in disarray, swamped by cheap imports from China and unable to compete because of onerous labor laws and outrageously high energy costs delivered by the green lobby.

Meanwhile, France has been beset by rioters supposedly wanting more money for education but really seeking even more cradle-to-grave handouts from a government that is now broke and can no longer bend to the people’s demands.

Most of the developed world is in trouble, but the U.S. has grown stronger and richer, thanks to the wealth created by the innovator class. Real disposable incomes have risen with Trump in the White House, with higher earnings, government handouts and lower taxes more than offsetting inflation. Employment is strong, manufacturing is expanding and productivity is soaring.

Let us hope overexcited Democrats do not destroy what is working. After all, the quickest way to lower prices is to bring on a recession. Surely that cannot be their elusive plan?

Liz Peek is a former partner of major bracket Wall Street firm Wertheim and Company.

articles.title: Judge temporarily blocks work on Trump arch after panel’s approval
articles.summary: A federal judge late Thursday ordered a pause on the construction of President Trump’s triumphal arch for 14 days. The temporary restraining order by U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan came shortly after the National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC) voted to approve the administration’s plans to build the arch between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery…
articles.body:
A federal judge late Thursday ordered a pause on the construction of President Trump’s triumphal arch for 14 days.

The temporary restraining order by U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan came shortly after the National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC) voted to approve the administration’s plans to build the arch between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery in Washington, D.C.

The motion passed by an 8-4 vote on Thursday after more than 100 public remarks, mostly against the project, in a nine-hour meeting.

In a memorandum opinion filed with the order , Chutkan wrote that D.C. and Virginia — which sued the administration over the project last month — “have shown that construction of the Arch will cause harm by ‘clogging traffic, impeding disaster preparedness, and harming the environment,’ which will also ‘require both jurisdictions to expend resources to monitor and mitigate those impacts.’”

“First, the harm is certain,” the judge continued. “Second, the District and Virginia will incur significant unrecoverable costs.”

“These are not self-inflicted costs. When federal action causes a state to undertake ‘expenditures to mitigate and recover from harms that could have been prevented’ absent that action, the state suffers an injury to its proprietary interests,” she added.

The judge also ordered the government to file a status report by Nov. 9 to certify that they are complying with the order.

The White House, in a Friday morning post on the social platform X , called the arch a “Monument to the American Spirit.”

“The Military Triumphal Arch will honor the heroes who gave everything for our nation — a monumental tribute to America’s first 250 years & a symbol of the next 250,” the post said.

In a Thursday press release, Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.), who represents Virginia’s 8th District, which includes the Arlington National Cemetery and Ronald Reagan National Airport, thanked the judge for her order.

“Judge Chutkan’s injunction will properly restrain Trump’s rush to ignore and bypass legal barriers, overwhelming opposition from the people most affected, and glaring evidence of irreparable harm to national treasures like Arlington National Cemetery,” Beyer said in the release.

“I will do everything in my power alongside my colleagues in the Democratic majorities just elected to the next Congress to ensure that this wasteful, disrespectful monstrosity goes nowhere,” he added.

At Thursday’s virtual meeting, which initially crashed and resumed about 40 minutes later, the commissioners and NCPC Chair Mark Paoletta spoke out in favor of the arch.

Paoletta, who was appointed by Trump, cited the 1925 congressional authorization for the Arlington Memorial Bridge Commission. The president and administration have also previously leaned on the commission’s authorization as reason to continue the project.

Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), the ranking member of the House Natural Resources Committee, called on the panel to reject the final proposal to build the arch during the hearing.

“Our most revered presidents earned their place of honor,” Huffman said. “They didn’t try to bestow it on themselves with gaudy tributes. The monuments to them came later, after history had judged that they were deserved.”

articles.title: James Carville cautions Democrats to stay away from DEI policies after midterm victories
articles.summary: James Carville warns Democrats against reviving DEI and woke politics after their historic midterm victory, saying the country simply "hated it."
articles.body:
Veteran Democratic strategist James Carville warned Democrats against reviving DEI and woke policies after dominating the midterms, arguing these policies hurt the party.

Carville spoke with a panel on Thursday's episode of the "Politics War Room" podcast about the Democrats' midterm victories before responding to a statement from Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif. , declaring that "DEI is back."

"I really like him. He's a very personable man. I think these people are all wrong," Carville reacted. "They tried DEI. The country hated it. Just hated it. It cost us seats."

Carville agreed with comments from Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., dismissing "Woke 1" and argued that returning to those policies would take the party in the wrong direction.

"The DEI people asked me to honor your identity above your humanity. I cannot do that. To me, you're a human being first. And if we bring this bulls--- language back, we're going to pay for it," he said.

After the 2024 presidential election, Carville warned that the "stench" of woke politics would cling to the party like a foul smell on a shirt. While he said Democrats had made progress since then, he lamented that some were returning to those policies.

"We're finally washing the stench of defund the police , communities of color, or every idiotic jacka-- academic word that [they] could think of. And we got rid of it. And AOC is right. Woke one was some crazy s---. Let's all go back and do it," he said. "Let's have progressive taxation. Let's have pluralism in America. Let's get out of Iran. Let's open rural hospitals. Okay, these are things that we can agree on."

Carville explained that he is a liberal, not a progressive, and wants to help rural Americans who may feel abandoned by the Democratic Party.

"I think rural America is the most forgotten part of America," he said, warning that his fellow Democrats need to be "talking about the problems of rural America or rural hospitals or rural education or rural libraries or anything else."

"And I think to the extent that this whole thing strikes people as another coastal people trying to impose something on the rest of the country, and the rest of the country doesn't want this, and now we're talking about bringing it back?" he warned.

Democrat Dan Turrentine, a co-host of "The Huddle," told Fox News Digital that Democrats largely abandoned social issues leading up to the midterms and focused on the economy and tackling "corruption."

"Not a single new member from a competitive state or district ran on restoring DEI. Quite the contrary, they stayed away from relitigating settled social issues and focused like a laser beam on costs, chaos, and corruption," Turrentine wrote. "Many people on our side are considering running for president and, in an effort to create a spark, will say controversial things to select audiences. The winning candidate will be focused on a broad coalition and keep the main things the main thing."

articles.body: WASHINGTON — John D. “Jay” Rockefeller IV, the progeny of one of America’s most famous and wealthiest families who during three decades in the Senate sought expanded healthcare for the poor and excoriated President George W. Bush’s handling of the Iraq War, died Friday at his home in Washington, The Washington Post reported. He was 89. His family did not ​provide a cause, the newspaper added. Rockefeller, a tall, soft-spoken Democrat with liberal views, was elected in 1984 to the first of his five six-year terms representing West Virginia ‌in the Senate after two terms as governor of the poor coal-mining state. Rockefeller voted in 2002 in favor of the Republican Bush’s measure authorizing the Iraq War, which began with a U.S.-led invasion in 2003. He later expressed regret over that vote and, as head of the Senate Intelligence Committee, accused Bush of taking the nation to war on “false premises.” He was a great-grandson of oil tycoon John D. Rockefeller and the scion of a family that formed a political ​dynasty that included his uncle, New York Gov. Nelson Rockefeller. New York-born Jay Rockefeller’s life changed direction after he graduated from Harvard University and served in a national service program in impoverished ​rural West Virginia from 1964 to 1966. When he was put in public office, he worked to increase healthcare access, fight poverty, provide health benefits to coal ⁠miners and assist military veterans. As a senator, he had a role in shaping the program created in 1997 under which the U.S. government helps states provide medical coverage for millions of uninsured ​children. Rockefeller backed Democratic President Bill Clinton’s failed proposal for near-universal health insurance coverage in the 1990s and then fought for Democratic President Barack Obama’s successful quest for a healthcare overhaul law, signed in 2010. In ​the debate over Obama’s measure, Rockefeller unsuccessfully sought to have the federal government offer a medical insurance program to the general population — in addition to existing programs for the poor and elderly — as an alternative to private insurance plans that could be costly and exclusive. “Championing those most in need has been my life’s calling and I will never stop fighting to make a difference for the people who mean so much to me,” Rockefeller said in 2013 when ​he announced at age 75 he would not seek a sixth Senate term. Before the Iraq invasion, Bush’s administration built the case for war by touting intelligence indicating Iraq owned an arsenal of weapons of ​mass destruction — they actually did not exist — and alleged ties between Iraqi leaders and the Al Qaeda network responsible for the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks on the U.S. The 9/11 Commission later found no credible evidence that Iraq was involved in the attacks. “If I had known then what I know now, I ‌would have voted ⁠against it,” Rockefeller told the Charleston Gazette newspaper in 2004, referring to the 2002 war authorization measure. “I think the intelligence was shaped,” he continued. “And I think the interpretation of the intelligence was shaped. You had a president who we now know was determined to go to war.” A report from the Intelligence Committee issued in 2008, when he served as its chairman, asserted that Bush, Vice President Dick Cheney and other leading officials exaggerated intelligence findings and ignored disputes within U.S. intelligence circles about Iraq’s weapons and the hotly disputed ties to Al Qaeda. The report rejected prewar statements by Bush and Cheney that ​Iraq might give Al Qaeda weapons of mass destruction. “Representing ​to the American people that the two ⁠had an operational partnership and posed a single, indistinguishable threat was fundamentally misleading and led the nation to war on false premises,” Rockefeller said as the report was released. During his Senate tenure, he also headed the Commerce, Science, Transportation and Veterans Affairs committees. Rockefeller was born June 18, 1937, weeks ​after the death of his great-grandfather, who had been America’s richest man. The Rockefeller name came with high expectations. His father was a famous philanthropist. ​His uncle Nelson Rockefeller served as ⁠vice president and governor of New York. His uncle David Rockefeller headed Chase Manhattan Bank and uncle Winthrop Rockefeller was governor of Arkansas. He was elected to West Virginia’s legislature in 1966 before age 30, then elected West Virginia’s secretary of state in 1968. He lost a bid to become governor in 1972, then served as a college president before being elected governor in 1976. Rockefeller, who became one of the wealthiest ⁠members of Congress, spent millions of dollars of his own money to bankroll his successful campaign for Senate ​in 1984. Rockefeller sometimes found himself overshadowed by his state’s other senator, Robert Byrd, who died in 2010 at age 92 as the longest-serving member of Congress in U.S. history. He usually backed his state’s coal and steel industries but angered coal executives in ​2012 by fighting Republican efforts to prevent regulation of emissions from coal-fired power plants. He was married to public television executive Sharon Percy Rockefeller, with whom he had four children.

articles.title: LEE CARTER: Socialism means two wildly different things to Republicans and Democrats
articles.summary: Gallup polling shows 65% of Democrats view socialism positively, but they're describing affordable healthcare and fairness, not the Soviet Union.
articles.body: Socialism is back. And judging by the reaction in some Republican circles, so is the Soviet Union. There is just one problem. Americans embracing socialism may not be talking about the socialism Republicans think they’re talking about. MAJORITY OF AMERICANS BROADLY REJECT SOCIALIST IDEOLOGY EVEN AS FAR LEFT SURGES TO POWER And if we don’t understand that, we’re going to miss one of the most important lessons of this election. I’m a researcher and strategist. I spend my life studying what people believe, why they believe it, and how the same words can mean wildly different things to different people. And right now, there may be no word in American politics more misunderstood than socialism. To many Republicans, socialism means communism. Government control. Breadlines. Moscow. A dreary existence in which everyone is equally miserable except the people running the government. To many Democrats, it means something else entirely. Affordable healthcare. A decent retirement. A fair shot at getting ahead. An economy where billionaires don’t get every break while everyone else gets the bill. Same word. Different movie. And the polling is remarkable. SOCIALISM SURGES AMONG DEMOCRATS AS PARTY LEADERS REJECT DSA AGENDA: ‘PACK OF FOOLS’ According to Gallup, 65% of Democrats have a positive view of socialism. So do 45% of independents. Only 14% of Republicans agree. But here’s the really interesting part. When Gallup asked Americans what they actually liked about socialism, Democrats and independents talked about access to basic services, economic equality, and a stronger safety net. They weren’t describing the Soviet Union. If we’re going to have that argument, shouldn’t we first make sure we’re having the same conversation? They were describing a country where ordinary people can afford to live. Now, that doesn’t mean socialism is simply another word for fairness. It is a real economic philosophy with real policy implications, and Americans have legitimate disagreements about what government should own, control, regulate, and provide. But if we’re going to have that argument, shouldn’t we first make sure we’re having the same conversation? Because right now, one side is warning about Vladimir Lenin while the other is worried about the price of lettuce. And the lettuce is winning. The irony of it all is that Trump messaged this before the Democrats did. He understood something fundamental about American voters in 2016. People were angry. LIBERAL-CITY RESIDENT HESITATES WHEN PRESSED ON BELIEFS: 'I HADN'T REALLY THOUGHT ABOUT SOCIALISM THAT WAY' They believed the system was rigged. They believed the powerful were getting richer while everyone else was falling behind. They believed Washington had become a private club where the members took care of themselves and sent the bill to the rest of the country. Trump promised to drain the swamp. He promised to fight for the forgotten man and woman. He promised to take on an establishment that had stopped listening. It was an extraordinarily powerful message. And now Democrats are making a strikingly similar argument about an economy that favors the wealthy, a political system that protects insiders, and ordinary Americans who can’t seem to get ahead. The vocabulary is different. The policy prescriptions are different. But the underlying frustration sounds awfully familiar. The swamp is still there. The rent is still due. The grocery bill is still too high. And voters are still asking the same question. Who’s fighting for me? That is the question both parties should be trying to answer. SOCIALISM'S GROWING APPEAL MEETS AN AWKWARD REALITY CHECK ON COLLEGE CAMPUS Not whether they can attach the most frightening label to the other side. Not whether they can win a debate about economic philosophy that most Americans haven’t had since freshman year. But whether they can make life more affordable, opportunity more accessible, and government more accountable. Because here’s what politicians consistently underestimate. Voters don’t experience the economy as an ideology. They experience it at the grocery store. At the pharmacy. When the mortgage payment comes due. When their children graduate from college with debt and move back into their childhood bedrooms. DEMOCRATS SAY THEY'LL MAKE LIFE AFFORDABLE. YOUR WALLET MAY DISAGREE You can tell someone they’re living under capitalism or socialism or democratic socialism. They’re still going to want to know why a carton of eggs costs so much. And before Republicans assume that attacking socialism is sufficient to win back voters, they might consider what those voters believe they’re supporting. You can oppose government ownership of industry and still believe Americans deserve affordable healthcare. You can support free enterprise and still think the economic system is tilted toward the wealthy. You can believe deeply in capitalism and still wonder why working hard doesn’t seem to get you as far as it used to. LIBERAL HOT SPOT RESIDENTS CAN’T AGREE ON WHAT SOCIALISM MEANS AS FAR-LEFT MOVEMENTS GAINS STEAM These aren’t necessarily contradictions. They’re the complicated, sometimes messy beliefs of real people. And they are exactly why persuasion remains possible. The lesson of this election isn’t that America has suddenly become socialist. It isn’t that capitalism has lost. JONATHAN TURLEY: SOCIALISM IS BACK IN STYLE AND DEMOCRATS ARE BUYING THE PITCH And it certainly isn’t that every candidate who talks about fairness has discovered some magical formula for political success. It’s that the argument over what fairness means, and who is delivering it, is very much alive. And that argument cannot be won simply by shouting a word louder. There is an important lesson here for Democrats, too. A positive view of socialism is not a blank check for every policy proposed in its name. Americans can support a stronger safety net while remaining deeply skeptical of government bureaucracy, higher taxes, or promises that sound wonderful until someone explains how much they cost. The label doesn’t do the work. The idea has to. That’s the part I hope both parties understand. For Republicans, the challenge is to explain how their vision of free enterprise can deliver the affordability and opportunity people are demanding. For Democrats, the challenge is to demonstrate that their promises of fairness can produce real results without creating a whole new set of problems. Neither side gets to skip the hard part. DEPROGRAMMED: SHE WAS ALL IN FOR SOCIALISM - UNTIL THE 'RED FLAGS' BECAME IMPOSSIBLE TO IGNORE Because Americans aren’t asking for a lecture on economic theory. They’re asking for a fair shot. And here’s the irony. The political language that helped propel Donald Trump to the White House — fighting for forgotten Americans, challenging powerful insiders, and taking on a rigged system — is now being echoed by some of the very Democrats who built their political identities opposing him. Different messengers. Different solutions. Familiar frustration. Perhaps the most important question coming out of this election isn’t whether America is embracing socialism. Perhaps it’s whether either party fully understands why so many Americans feel the economy isn’t working for them. Because you don’t defeat an idea by attacking its name. You defeat it by offering people something better. And you don’t win lasting support by telling voters what they should be afraid of. You earn it by giving them something to believe in. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION The American people aren’t asking for a return to Moscow. They’re asking for a country where hard work pays off, opportunity isn’t reserved for the well-connected, and getting ahead doesn’t feel like winning the lottery. Call that fairness. Call it opportunity. Call it the American Dream. Just don’t make the mistake of thinking that winning an argument over the word socialism means you’ve answered the people who find it appealing. Because the next election won’t be decided in a political science classroom. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP It will be decided by Americans who want to know whether their lives are getting better. And they are going to listen to whoever has a convincing answer. articles.title: Veto or deals: Can Trump find a way to work with Democrats?
articles.summary: Trump has three options to affect legislation, say analysts: veto legislation, enforce executive orders or make deals.
articles.body:
As the United States midterm election results landed late on Tuesday night, United States President Donald Trump took a phone call from the news outlet Politico.

A wave for the Democratic Party had sunk Trump’s Republican Party. For the first time in his two stints as president, Trump’s Republican Party no longer controlled either chamber of Congress.

But in the phone interview, Trump put on a brave face — and offered an olive branch: He said that he would be willing to work with Democrats .

“They’ve already called, and they want to work with me. I have the right to veto everything, but I don’t want to be just sitting there for two years just vetoing everything,” he said.

While a handful of seats remain to be counted, the Democrats have won comfortable majorities in both the House of Representatives, where they have secured at least 253 seats out of 435, and in the Senate, where they have won at least 54 out of 100.

Trump has since posted a picture on his Truth Social account using the Make America Great Again red baseball hat to read “VETO”. Despite the Democrats’ success, as president, Trump holds broad executive authority, with Article 1, Section 7 of the US Constitution stipulating that the president has the power to reject legislation passed by Congress through a veto.

Congress can override the veto, but would need to have a two-thirds majority, something that the Democrats do not have in either chamber.

But Trump’s comments to Politico underscore an alternate possibility — the president may pick and choose when to veto, and when to work with Democrats.

As it stands, Trump has three options: veto legislation, enforce executive orders or make deals.

Since Trump was inaugurated in January 2025, he has passed 292 executive orders: 67 this year and 225 last year, according to the Federal Register.

But now, according to Andrew Proctor, a lecturer in US politics at University College London, Trump has even less leverage than before with Congress.

“I think the biggest thing is we’re probably going to see a decent amount of gridlock. The Democrats are going to try to pass policies, but he’s got the power to veto them, and Democrats don’t have enough seats in either chamber to overcome any vetoes that he has,” Proctor said.

“So that raises questions about, will he try to work with the Democrats at all on passing legislation? I think recent history says that’s unlikely.”

Still, some Democrats have said that they would work with the president to advance programmes central to their campaign promises.

Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed, the first Muslim elected to the US Senate, has already said he could work with Trump — even though the US president had used racist and Islamophobic rhetoric to target El-Sayed during the campaign.

El-Sayed told MSNOW on Thursday that if Trump was interested in “getting money out of politics, putting money in pockets and passing Medicare for All, that’s what I ran to do, and I’m looking forward to working with anyone who is willing to do that”.

“He is the president of the United States,” he said. “I’m going to be one United States senator, and if he’s interested in working on issues that I want to work on – getting more people healthcare, ending the Medicare cuts, ending the stupid war, stopping these stupid tariffs with Canada – then let’s talk about doing that and go and deliver for the public.”

Progressive Senator Bernie Sanders has also said, in recent interviews, that he would not rule out Trump signing onto a Medicare for All bill if Democrats pass it in both chambers of Congress. He described Trump as a “politician” who was not “too ideological”.

Proctor argued that Trump could indeed make a deal with the Democrats based on how good it could make him look, but that getting Medicare for All passed in the next two years appeared unlikely.

“I do think that a place where common ground could emerge on healthcare is rolling back, specifically the sort of subsidies that were cut” under Trump’s earlier legislation , he said. “So that would make healthcare more affordable for millions of Americans.”

Proctor pointed out that some Republicans in 2025 had said they were willing to negotiate with Democrats on healthcare reforms.

“That didn’t end up happening, but I could imagine that might be a place for healthcare-specific policy where we could see something emerge,” he said. “I don’t think that a broader healthcare debate on passing Medicare for All, though, is really in the cards.”

Though Trump has said he would be willing to use veto, he has historically not been among the most avid proponents of the practice.

He has so far used the veto twice in this term, and used it 10 times during his first term. Joe Biden used it 12 times in his single term, while Barack Obama used the veto a dozen times over two terms.

Overall, the presidential use of the veto has declined with time: Bill Clinton vetoed legislation 37 times between 1993 and 2001. His predecessor, George HW Bush, used it 44 times in his single term — almost once a month. Ronald Reagan used it 78 times over his two terms.

But Proctor said that Republicans also have a different tool to try and block legislation. That is the filibuster, a tactic that delays a vote on a specific piece of legislation by using an extended debate, which would impact the Democrats’ ability to get something passed.

“This is what they did to [former President Barack] Obama,” Proctor told Al Jazeera. “Senate Republicans will probably try to do the same thing, and it also means that we don’t even get to the point of Trump having the power to veto because the legislation never reaches him in the first place.”

Since the Democrats swept the midterms on Tuesday, calls for investigations against the administration have already emerged.

In his first term, Trump was impeached twice — first for the abuse of power and obstruction of Congress, and the second time for “inciting” the US Capitol riots.

On Tuesday night, US Representative Robert Garcia, who is set to become chairman of the House Oversight Committee, wrote on X: “LAWYER UP.” Senator Ron Wyden, who is expected to lead the Senate Finance Committee, wrote in a post on X: “Subpoenas.”

However, the Trump administration has already denied any wrongdoing.

“If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people,” said White House spokesperson Lauren Bis on Wednesday.

Reports also suggest that impeachment proceedings against Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth might be imminent, over the Iran war that Trump and other Republicans have blamed for the party’s losses.

articles.title: Bitter Fetterman-El-Sayed feud threatens to complicate Schumer's Senate unity push
articles.summary: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer's Party unity push faces an early test as John Fetterman and Abdul El-Sayed trade insults over U.S. aid to Israel.
articles.body: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer called for Democratic Party unity Wednesday following the midterm elections, but a bitter feud between Sen. John Fetterman and Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed could complicate efforts to unite the caucus in the 120th Congress. The two Democrats traded personal insults throughout the 2026 election cycle, clashing over U.S. military assistance to Israel, Medicare for All and the ideological direction of the Democratic Party. "You put one ogre on a pike, and then everyone else gets the message," El-Sayed, D-Mich., reportedly told progressive donors during a private Zoom call, arguing that challenging moderate Democrats in primary elections would send a message to the party's establishment. CHUCK SCHUMER AFTER SWEEPING DEMOCRATIC MIDTERM VICTORIES: 'I'LL BE RE-ELECTED AS MAJORITY LEADER' Fetterman, D-Pa., has been an outspoken supporter of U.S. military assistance to Israel, including funding for its Iron Dome missile defense system, and he has backed military action against Hezbollah and Iran. El-Sayed, meanwhile, campaigned against the war in Iran and opposed taxpayer-funded military operations and U.S. aid to Israel. A longtime Democratic Senate staffer told Fox News Digital that they would "not be surprised" if tensions emerged between the two lawmakers but expressed confidence that their loyalty to the Democratic Party would outweigh their personal disagreements. FETTERMAN CLAIMS DEMOCRATIC ‘BIG TENT’ HAS MORE ROOM FOR ‘AMERICA DESERVED 9/11’ THAN ISRAEL SUPPORT The staffer added that Fetterman has faced criticism from other members of the Senate Democratic caucus, though those disagreements have not necessarily prevented lawmakers from working together. During a televised primary debate, El-Sayed confirmed that his "ogre on a pike" remark was directed at Fetterman, accusing the Pennsylvania senator of having "abandoned his elected values" through his support for U.S. military assistance to Israel. DEMS CLASH OVER AIPAC MONEY, ‘OGRE’ ATTACK AND ELECTABILITY DURING CRUCIAL SENATE DEBATE El-Sayed later doubled down on his criticism, arguing against funding foreign defense systems such as Israel's Iron Dome while American schools struggle with limited resources. Fetterman fired back, referring to El-Sayed as the "Pontiac Platner" in an apparent jab at the Maine Democrat Graham Platner, who dropped out of his Senate race this election season under the weight of multiple scandals. FETTERMAN 'DARES' EL-SAYED TO STICK WITH PIKER, CLAIMS MICHIGAN NOMINEE HAS 'LITTLE MAN SYNDROME ENERGY' The Pennsylvania senator also accused El-Sayed of seeking to become the "head of our emerging pro-Hamas wing here in the party," criticizing his positions on Israel. El-Sayed's campaign appearances with left-wing streamer Hasan Piker, who previously said "America deserved 9/11," further fueled the dispute, prompting Fetterman to publicly condemn Piker's remarks. The tensions escalated after El-Sayed narrowly defeated Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., in the Democratic primary by less than one percentage point. Days before the general election, reports emerged that El-Sayed's campaign had barred Stevens from attending its final campaign events, drawing another sharp rebuke from Fetterman. MICHIGAN DEMOCRAT HALEY STEVENS BACKS EL-SAYED AFTER NARROW PRIMARY DEFEAT, CALLS SOCIALISM ‘DANGEROUS’ "Rep. Haley Stevens simply held Abdul El-Sayed accountable for his views on Israel and fixation with Jewish money. El-Sayed is going after a woman and banning her from campaign events for having an opinion," Fetterman told Jewish Insider. "He has the worst case of little man syndrome I've ever seen," Fetterman added. DEM INSURGENT TURNS ON THE CHARM WITH PARTY ESTABLISHMENT AS SCHUMER LEAVES BITTER FEUD HANGING Despite the public hostility, the Democratic Senate staffer's assessment suggests the two lawmakers could ultimately set aside their differences to advance their party's legislative priorities. The feud could nevertheless present an early test for Schumer, D-N.Y., as he seeks to maintain unity among Senate Democrats, particularly on divisive issues such as U.S. foreign policy and the party's progressive agenda. articles.title: 'We didn't expect this': Texas Democrats stunned as blue wave topples GOP stronghold
articles.summary: Texas Democrat James Talarico toppled Ken Paxton by over 12 points as a blue wave shattered the GOP's grip on the deep -red Lone Star State.
articles.body: AUSTIN, Texas — As the Democrats’ blue wave began to slam into Texas, Richard Torres, a Texan who has voted blue his entire life, kept peering at the results pouring in on reporters’ screens all around him. And when it was announced Texas state Rep. James Talarico had toppled Ken Paxton, he sat down to take it in. Torres was the former chair of the Williamson County Democratic Party, where Talarico grew up and attended high school in Round Rock, Texas. He never thought that Texas Republicans would be swept away by the oncoming blue wave. TEXAS' RED WALL FACING ITS BIGGEST THREAT IN DECADES AS REPUBLICANS SCRAMBLE TO DEFEND IT "We started seeing some changes, but not what we expected tonight," Torres told Fox News Digital. "We didn't expect this tonight." When asked why a deep-red stronghold like the Lone Star State had become so rapidly blue, Torres said that it started at the top with President Donald Trump and should serve as a message to GOP candidates and officials across the state. "I think it sends a message that they're on the wrong track, and they've been for a while, but they won't accept the problems we have with the president," Torres said. "They're totally supporting him. I don't know why." "But they don't see the problems that we're having in this country with all the things that have happened with the war going on and things of this type," he continued. "And they just seem to support him on it. This is a referendum against Trump." STATE OF PLAY: BLUE WAVE SWEEPS DEMOCRATS INTO POWER, WITH KEY RACES STILL HANGING IN BALANCE Talarico and several other Democratic candidates, including Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, shattered the GOP’s grip on Texas, serving Republicans in Congress a stiff blow as their majorities in both chambers rapidly evaporated Tuesday night. And the incoming lawmaker didn’t just squeak by Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. He beat the Trump-backed candidate, who was not the first choice of Republicans in Washington, by over 12 percentage points, or well over 1 million votes, in a state that Trump won in 2024 by nearly 14 points. To secure that win, Talarico needed to capture Republicans and Democrats in Texas. One of those Republicans, James, told Fox News Digital that he had always voted for the GOP until this election. TEXAS SENATE VICTOR JAMES TALARICO LAYS OUT COMMON GROUND WITH TRUMP, VOWS TO 'WORK TOGETHER' "I've been a Republican my whole life, but I'm voting Democratic this year because I think we need to," James said. "The Republicans have lost their way, I believe." While the optimism at the watch party was palpable, be it through the pumping music or over half a dozen mobile bars with lines dozens of people deep, there was still a cautious anxiety among some voters. Particularly after Democrats had gotten so close to flipping the Senate seat before in 2018, when former Texas state Rep. Beto O’Rourke gave Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, a run for his money. O’Rourke would end up losing by roughly two points, but the exuberance that turned to heartbreak wasn’t soon forgotten by the Lone Star State’s Democratic voters. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP As results began to roll in and the crowd’s energy began to explode, Beverly, another longtime Texas resident and voter, said Tuesday night was bigger than Texas. "This feels like a now or never moment in the entire United States," she said. "We either turn things around or we might as well kiss it all goodbye."

articles.title: Former US senator and West Virginia governor Jay Rockefeller dies at 89
articles.summary: Political figures issued statements honoring former Democratic U.S. senator and West Virginia Gov. Jay Rockefeller, who passed away at the age of 89 years old.
articles.body: Former U.S. Senator and West Virginia governor John D. "Jay" Rockefeller IV has died at the age of 89. The Democratic political figure was from the prominent Rockefeller family of New York. He served in the Senate for just shy of 30 years. WHAT THE 2026 MIDTERM RESULTS MEAN FOR CAPITOL HILL West Virginia polititical figures spoke highly of Rockefeller in statements on Friday. Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.V., said in a post on X, "Deeply saddened by the passing of former Senator and Governor Jay Rockefeller. Jay dedicated his life to serving West Virginia and our nation, leaving a lasting legacy. He was always a true gentleman who treated me with respect, kindness, and encouragement. "Over the years, we developed a wonderful friendship that transcended politics, and I will always be grateful for that. Above all, Jay loved his family. Charlie and I are keeping Sharon, their children and grandchildren, and the entire Rockefeller family in our prayers," she added. FORMER GOP WHIP, ARIZONA SEN JON KYL DEAD AT 84 Former Sen. Joe Manchin, who is also a former West Virginia governor, described Rockefeller as a "mentor." "I looked up to Jay as a mentor and as a friend. When I ran for my first full term in the U.S. Senate in 2012, Jay was on the front lines and helped me every step of the way. He showed me how to be an effective U.S. Senator and best represent our state. He couldn’t have been a better mentor or tutor," Manchin wrote in part of a longer post on X. Manchin, a longtime Democrat, announced toward the end of his Senate tenure that he switched "to register as an independent with no party affiliation." ROCKEFELLER HEIR VANISHED IN TRIBAL WATERS AFTER EERIE LAST WORDS CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Sen. Jim Justice, R-W.V., also commented on Rockefeller's death, noting in a post on X, "Senator Jay Rockefeller’s passing is sad news to all of West Virginia. His years of dedicated service as Governor and Senator truly reflect the love he had for his great state. Senator Rockefeller worked hard for West Virginians and made a difference in countless lives. Cathy and I send our deepest love and prayers to Sharon, their children, and the entire Rockefeller family." Justice, who is also a former governor, won one West Virginia gubernatorial race as a Democrat then later won another contest as a Republican. Current Gov. Patrick Morrisey, who is a Republican, said in part of a statement that Rockefeller's "work helped shape our state and left a lasting mark on the lives of generations of West Virginians. His decades of service deserve our respect and gratitude, and his legacy will remain an important part of West Virginia's history."

articles.title: Progressive group's 182-page blueprint maps out potential Dem investigations into Trump, corporate allies
articles.summary: Former President Joe Biden aides mapped Tesla, Apple, Amazon and OpenAI as targets for sweeping Democratic congressional investigations into Trump allies.
articles.body: A progressive policy organization led by former aides to President Joe Biden and former aides to progressive Sens. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass. assembled a detailed blueprint for potential Democratic congressional investigations to target President Donald Trump and his allies beyond the White House, which could foreshadow the goals of the 120th Congress. Groundwork Collaborative's dossier, obtained and analyzed by Fox News Digital, maps Trump donors and corporate allies for potential Democratic congressional investigations. Leaders in big tech and CEOs of large corporations are likely to be among the targets of the anti-Trump crusade. A longtime Democratic Senate staffer familiar with the process told Fox News Digital that the Democratic majorities on these committees already plan to exclusively focus on targeting allies and donors of the president, going as far as targeting the ones who donated to the new White House ballroom, once they move into the majority. HOUSE GOP LAUNCHES DEFENSE PLAN TO SHIELD TRUMP FROM LOOMING DEMOCRAT INVESTIGATIONS However, the staffer did not see the document, which specifically says to target those who gave to the ballroom, library, Trump’s inauguration and campaign. Reports had said it was obtained by House committees as well, but a House Judiciary Committee aide for Democrats told Semafor it was "one of many" and dismissed it, saying, "We all get a lot of emails." But nevertheless, it could still show signs of where people on the left want the new Democratic majorities to go. Other plans outlined in the document include targeting Trump-aligned corporations, such as Tesla, Apple, Amazon, Oracle, Trump Media and World Liberty Financial. The letter also mentions Palantir's Alex Karp and Coinbase's Brian Armstrong by name, with possible hearings involving executives from OpenAI, Meta, Google, Microsoft, Oracle and others. TAX BREAKS HELPING FUEL TRUMP'S LATEST TECH PUSH JUST LANDED IN DEMS' CROSSHAIRS Other priorities include investigating Trump's personal finances, proposing congressional scrutiny of Trump's tax arrangements, cryptocurrency businesses and alleged preferential treatment of corporate donors. The document continues, urging the committees to expand federal oversight of artificial intelligence, outline investigations into AI companies and proposals to restrict algorithmic pricing, workplace surveillance and certain autonomous AI technologies. This includes investigating the Trump administration's Medicare AI program, which uses the WISeR model, employing artificial intelligence systems to screen prior authorization requests in traditional Medicare to determine whether specific outpatient procedures are medically necessary. The document adds that committees should increase scrutiny of private businesses through hearings, document demands and potential legislation targeting major employers, landlords, insurers and technology companies. TRUMP CMS FACES BIPARTISAN PUSHBACK OVER MEDICARE PROPOSAL TIED TO BIDEN-ERA DRUG PRICING LAW "We just had a midterm election where Democratic candidates across the country made the point that corporations have been doing very well for the last several years, while the typical family has been getting squeezed with higher prices and worse service," Bharat Ramamurti, a former deputy director of the National Economic Council who coordinated with Groundwork on the dossier, told Fox News Digital. "The oversight agenda is about trying to understand and figure out what exactly are these corporations doing, who's responsible for these decisions, and then what, as policymakers, can folks in Congress do about it," Ramamurti added. Pages later in the document also mention plans for restricting corporate ownership and pricing practices. It discusses measures aimed at institutional housing investors, algorithmic rent-setting and corporate pricing systems. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The document proposes investigating a reported settlement involving Trump's tax audits, including requesting information about the Chicago tower audit and questioning Treasury officials. Elizabeth Elkind contributed to this report.

articles.title: Xavier García Albiol, sobre que España renuncie al Mundial 2030 si la final se disputa en Marruecos en lugar de en nuestro país: “Totalmente de acuerdo”
articles.standfirst: El alcalde Badalona ha dejado su reflexión en su cuenta oficial de X
articles.summary: El alcalde Badalona ha dejado su reflexión en su cuenta oficial de X
articles.body: En declaraciones a ‘El Chiringuito’, el espacio deportivo presentado por Josep Pedrerol, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, líder del Partido Popular, afirmó que España debe renunciar al Mundial 2030 si la final se disputa en Marruecos en lugar de en nuestro país. Estas palabras han generado muchas reacciones, algunas en contra, y otras que siguen su misma línea. Un ejemplo de esto último es la reflexión de Xavier García Albiol. El alcalde de Badalona e integrante del PP ha compartido su visión en su cuenta oficial de X. “Hola a todos, mirad, os voy a hablar de fútbol. Os hablo como aficionado y también, evidentemente, como candidato al congreso del Partido Popular en la provincia de Barcelona. Feijóo ha hecho una propuesta que yo, como aficionado y como político, evidentemente, pero sobre todo como aficionado estoy totalmente de acuerdo”, comienza diciendo. “Resulta que, como sabéis, el próximo Mundial de Fútbol lo organizaba España y Portugal, era organizado por los dos países. Y Pedro Sánchez, sin consultar a nadie, hizo una oferta pública de invitar a Marruecos a que también participase en la organización del Mundial. Bien, esto lo hizo, repito, sin avisar a la federación y sin avisar absolutamente a nadie” prosigue, poniendo contexto. Albiol califica esta acción de Sánchez como “un auténtico despropósito”, “una barbaridad” y “una deslealtad”, además de poner sobre la mesa otra pregunta: “¿Cómo es posible que Marruecos no tenga dinero para mantener a la gente que viene de manera ilegal? Muchos de ellos vienen de manera ilegal a España y, en cambio, si tienen dinero para gastárselo, tienen miles de millones para gastárselo en construcciones de estadios de fútbol”. “Todo es absolutamente disparatado, pero sobre todo, lo que me parece peor de todos es esa falta de personalidad, esa falta de dignidad por parte de Pedro Sánchez haciendo este movimiento. Por tanto, estoy totalmente de acuerdo con Feijóo. La final es nuestra, los organizadores somos nosotros, Sánchez nos metió en un lío y no podemos permitir que se nos humille de esa manera”, sentenciaba el integrante del PP.

articles.title: Red states have spent decades dominating a key corner of the economy — will the blue wave change that?
articles.summary: The "Crazy Rich Texans" trend is backed by data as a study of 24,000 transactions shows red states outpacing blue states in real estate returns.
articles.body: DALLAS — Red states have quietly outpaced their blue-state counterparts in commercial real estate investment returns for years, according to a new study highlighting stark differences in state economic policies. But sweeping Democratic gains in Tuesday's midterm elections — even in traditionally deep-red strongholds — are raising questions about whether those states can maintain their economic advantages as the political landscape shifts in the new year. Mitch Flax, founder and chief investment officer of Net Equity Capital, told Fox News Digital his research was sparked by the observation that commercial real estate investors based in blue states were reluctant to invest in their own markets. The findings underscore a broader economic battle playing out across the country as businesses and wealthy Americans relocate across state lines, bringing jobs, investment dollars and tax revenue with them while potentially leaving financial holes in the states they abandon. CEO SAYS DOING BUSINESS IN STATE ‘SUCKS’ AS COMPANY HEADS TO TEXAS AMID CALIFORNIA EXODUS "I had a large family office based out of Chicago who lives in California who said, we don't invest in real estate in blue states," Flax recalled. Coming on the heels of the 2026 midterms, the study also raises questions about whether the state-level tax and business policies that have helped fuel growth in red states will remain intact as Democrats make political gains and begin to enact their agenda. The encounter prompted Flax to examine nearly 24,000 commercial real estate transactions to determine whether political differences between states were associated with investment performance. Researchers used a proxy to estimate returns and classified states as red or blue based on their votes in the 2024 presidential election. Flax attributed the performance gap identified in his analysis largely to differences in state-level business policies, arguing that those policies influence where companies relocate, jobs are created and, ultimately, where capital flows. AMERICA’S NEXT ECONOMIC POWERHOUSE MAY BE RISING IN RED-STATE TERRITORY The findings come as corporate migration toward lower-tax states rose in recent years, with Texas emerging as a major destination for companies relocating from costly coastal hubs. Flax says that Texas is on track to be the next Singapore-style "tax haven" for companies, due to its policies attracting business and industry. "We've all seen the movie ‘Crazy Rich Asians’ — get ready for Crazy Rich Texans, because that movie is coming," he said. It's unclear how Tuesday's results will impact that prediction after Texas flipped a U.S. Senate seat blue with Senator-elect James Talarico beating Ken Paxton, who was backed by President Donald Trump, and Democrat Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa beating Republican Gov. Greg Abbott. As Fox News Digital previously reported, a CBRE analysis found that 725 companies relocated their headquarters between 2018 and 2025. Dallas-Fort Worth led the nation with 111 relocations, followed by Austin with 88 and Houston with 31. Meanwhile, the San Francisco Bay Area, a deep blue enclave, recorded a net loss of 163 corporate headquarters during the same period, as companies cited taxes, labor regulations and rising living costs among their reasons for leaving. THIS STATE ISN’T JUST GROWING — ITS ECONOMY IS GETTING RICHER PER RESIDENT Flax, however, also argued that population shifts and corporate relocations are symptoms of a deeper economic divide, with underlying business policies shaping investment decisions and determining where capital flows. "Most of the large asset managers out there are underwriting population in this migration flow. But the reality is that's a symptom," Flax told Fox News Digital. "When you look at exactly what's causing it, it's pure structural business policy," he added. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Flax said those policies can trigger a ripple effect across the commercial real estate market as businesses relocate, workers follow and demand grows for housing, retail and office space. "Migration is the symptom, but it's a cascade, right? So policy draws people and companies and then every kind of commercial real estate follows," Flax said. "Apartments follow migration, retail follows rooftops, office follows jobs, warehouse follows logistics."

articles.title: Musk says Tesla to wind down polarising Cybertruck production as sales lag
articles.summary: Released in 2023, the truck has become a symbol to some of opposition to Musk amid foray into US politics.
articles.body:
Tesla CEO Elon Musk has said the company will wind down production of Cybertrucks at its Texas facility amid poor sales.

Trillionaire Musk made the announcement in a post on X on Friday, saying the wind-down would enable the company to increase its production of the new Cybercab model, launched as part of a foray into the so-called robo-taxi industry.

“Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production,” Musk wrote.

Announced in 2019, the Cybertruck’s stark design, featuring an angular stainless steel exterior, proved immediately polarising .

At an unveiling ceremony that year, Musk sought to prove its windows were shatterproof. But the exhibition backfired, with metal balls launched at the car cracking two of the windows.

The vehicle quickly became a symbol of opposition to Musk as he became increasingly involved in United States politics, including briefly leading the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) panel tasked by the administration of US President Donald Trump with cleaving federal government agencies.

Musk most recently spent nearly half a billion dollars in the US midterm election campaign in support of Republican candidates, including more than $200 million in support of the failed Senate candidacy of Republican Ken Paxton in Texas. Beyond Tesla, Musk’s SpaceX company is also based in Texas.

But the spending did little to prevent a blue wave in US politics, which saw Democrats take commanding control of the US House of Representatives and Senate. The shift could spell investigations into Musk’s work with the federal government.

Musk had initially predicted the Cybertrucks, which became available to consumers at the end of 2023, would sell at a rate of about 250,000 a year.

The model fell far below that target. In 2024, about 38,965 units were sold. That figure declined by nearly half in 2025, with 20,237 sold.

In his announcement on Friday, Musk did not say whether Cybertruck manufacturing would shift to another factory. The plant in Texas is the only known production site.

In response to a user on X, Musk called the Cybertruck the “best vehicle Tesla has ever made”, hailing the “end of an era”.
