articles.title: 'Money out of politics' ballot measure sparks First Amendment fight in battleground state
articles.summary: Supporters say Proposal 2 curbs pay-to-play donations, but its critics argue it could impact policy research and other communications discussing candidates without telling voters how to vote.
articles.body: Michigan voters approved a ballot initiative called Proposal 2, pitched to them as a way to curb pay-to-play donations and get money out of politics. But the measure has also triggered a federal First Amendment lawsuit alleging its separate speech and disclosure provisions could ensnare journalists, nonprofits and policy researchers who discuss elected officials. Michiganders for Money Out of Politics, also known as MOP UP Michigan, said the lawsuit was expected after voters approved Proposal 2. Campaign manager Maura Cowley said the group is "confident Proposal 2 will withstand legal scrutiny" after organizers said they submitted more than 560,000 signatures to place the measure on the ballot. The Mackinac Center for Public Policy, which filed the lawsuit, says it is not challenging the initiative’s central pay-to-play restrictions on political contributions from utility companies and government contractors. Its lawsuit instead targets provisions imposing reporting and disclosure requirements on certain communications that refer to candidates or "promote, support, attack or oppose" candidates or ballot questions, even without expressly urging voters to support or oppose them. "Michigan voters deserve the freedom to research, debate, and report on the policies that shape their lives. But Proposal 2 is a Trojan horse: while it claims to target corruption, it would expose the Mackinac Center, its supporters, and ordinary Michiganders to criminal penalties and harassment simply for discussing public policy," Patrick Wright, the Mackinac Center’s vice president of legal affairs, said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital. SURVEY REVEALS COLLEGE STUDENTS' GROWING INTOLERANCE FOR FREE SPEECH Under Proposal 2, any person — not just a campaign or political committee — who makes "electioneering communications" aggregating at least $5,000 in a calendar year would have to file a report within 10 days. Additional reports would be required after each additional $5,000 in covered communications. The reports would include the dates and costs of the communications, candidates mentioned, vendors paid and information about donors who contributed more than $100 for the purpose of making the communications. Proposal 2 defines "electioneering communications" as public messages — including broadcasts, print publications, mailings, telephone calls, internet communications and other forms of general public communication — that reference a clearly identifiable candidate, regardless of whether they contain express advocacy, within 100 days of a general election or 30 days before a primary or special election. The communication must also be targeted to the relevant electorate where the candidate appears on the ballot, according to the provision. Mackinac argues the measure leaves important questions unanswered, including which expenses count toward the $5,000 threshold, what it means for a donor to contribute "for making electioneering communications," and how the state will determine whether a communication is targeted to the relevant electorate. SUPREME COURT STRIKES DOWN LIMIT ON PARTY CAMPAIGN SPENDING IN COORDINATION WITH CANDIDATES The Mackinac Center’s lawsuit also challenges Proposal 2’s expansion of the definition of an election-related "expenditure." The amended definition includes public communications that "promote, support, attack, or oppose" a candidate or ballot question, regardless of whether they expressly advocate for or against the outcome. Under the proposal’s revised committee definition, an organization that spends at least $500 on such expenditures could be treated as a political committee if the state determines the spending was intended to influence voters. Brett Nolan, an Institute for Free Speech attorney representing Mackinac, told Fox News Digital that the new electioneering-communications reporting provision contains no express exception for neutral reporting, legislative voting records or policy research. Proposal 2 does retain an existing exemption for certain news stories, commentary and editorials from being treated as campaign spending, but Mackinac argues that exemption does not resolve the reporting requirements for electioneering communications. Mackinac’s complaint points specifically to its MichiganVotes project, policy scorecards, a neutral policy brief about Proposal 2, magazines, radio programs, podcasts and public-policy events as examples of speech that could be swept up in the new requirements because those materials sometimes discuss elected officials or candidates. GOP LAWMAKERS URGE SUPREME COURT TO STRENGTHEN FIRST AMENDMENT PROTECTIONS FOR STREET PREACHERS "The Supreme Court has said several times in recent years that disclosure mandates like this create an 'inevitable' chilling effect on free speech because the risk of political harassment (or worse) is so significant. The more costs we impose on those who want to exchange ideas and discuss public policy, the fewer of those people we will have," Nolan said. "This law goes much further than addressing any interest the state may have in transparency about those who are funding campaigns and election advocacy," he continued. "The notion that the government has an interest in monitoring people who talk about public policy if they dare mention an elected official is antithetical to the First Amendment." The lawsuit against Proposal 2 seeks to block the electioneering-communications reporting requirement and the political-committee rules as applied to Mackinac — not to overturn Proposal 2 in its entirety. The measure is set to take effect 10 days after the official declaration of the vote, and no later than Dec. 3, according to the lawsuit. "This lawsuit is no surprise," Cowley said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "The corporations bankrolling our opposition have been gearing up for this lawsuit since Proposal 2 first qualified for the ballot, if not before." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER According to MOP UP Michigan, besides curbing pay-to-play political donations, Proposal 2 is designed to close what the group calls an "issue-ad loophole" — the ability to discuss candidates or ballot questions without expressly urging voters to support or oppose them in order to avoid certain disclosure rules. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Last night, Michiganders spoke loud and clear, voting to pass Proposal 2 with an overwhelming majority and delivering a resounding mandate to end pay-to-play politics and put power back where it belongs – with the people," Cowley continued. "The bottom line is that we are confident Proposal 2 will withstand legal scrutiny, and we were fully expecting and are prepared to take on this challenge."

articles.title: Could the US midterms put a pin in the AI bubble?
articles.summary: Fears of more AI regulation appear to have sparked fear among investors, but  concerns about the industry have been growing for some time.
articles.body:
Is the artificial intelligence (AI) gold rush coming to an end, or is this simply a reality check?

That's the question which is hanging over investors, and which has prompted steep falls on the world's stock markets.

The sell-off in the US on Thursday was most dramatic on the Nasdaq, home to tech industry titans such as Alphabet, Nvidia, Meta and Apple.

It followed sweeping gains by the Democrats in this week's mid-term elections in the US, which have given the party full control of Congress.

A number of leading Democrats campaigned against the unhindered expansion of data centres, which have underpinned the growth of artificial intelligence.

Fears this will lead to more regulation of AI appear to have sparked fear among investors. But concerns about the industry's prospects have been growing for some time.

The release of Chat GPT by Open AI in late 2022 is widely seen as having generated massive public and corporate interest in the practical uses of AI. It also sparked a modern-day gold rush.

Investors flocked to put their money into companies producing computer chips and networking infrastructure, building data centres and providing the energy to power them, as well as developing the AI itself. The value of tech companies soared.

The boom continued into this year. Investments in AI are expected to reach $1trillion in 2026 alone according to research by Goldman Sachs. The sector has scooped up so much available cash that other industries have seen their own borrowing costs increase as a result.

But investors want returns, and in recent months concerns have been growing about whether the AI boom can produce the expected riches.

Those worries have emerged at a time when public comments from AI researchers casting doubt over the safety of AI - even suggesting it could represent an existential threat to humanity - have been grabbing headlines and fuelling speculation that a clampdown could lie ahead.

US tech stocks edge back up after AI slowdown fears sent value of firms plummeting

How does it affect me if share prices fall?

These firms you've never heard of are feeding fears the AI bubble could burst

While the Trump administration has been all-in on AI, or "super intelligence" as the president likes to call it, many leading Democrats have tapped into grassroots concerns about the expansion of data centres and their impact on local communities.

These were largely focused on the facilities' high consumption of water and electricity, which many feared would push up their household bills – as well as the noise, use of land, and general disruption associated with them.

A Gallup poll published in May showed 71% of Americans would oppose the building of a data centre in their community. The figure for a nuclear power station was 53%.

James Talarico, who won the Senate race in once staunchly Republican Texas, was one of those to tap into this scepticism.

"While we want to protect America's leadership in artificial intelligence, we are still grappling with how it will affect everything from how we work to how our children learn," he said.

"We must protect Americans and establish clear, consistent laws for businesses."

With control of both houses of Congress, Democrats are now expected to challenge the president's technology agenda more vigorously, while introducing legislation which could curb the expansion of the industry.

Texas' Democratic governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned against data centres, pledging a moratorium on the construction of new facilities.

Hinojosa's win could present opposition to tech multi-billionaire Elon Musk, who has moved large parts of SpaceX and Tesla's operations to the state, for years a Republican stronghold.

The Tesla boss had spent nearly $450m to back Republican campaigns in the midterms.

As the co-founder of the British-based technology firm Arm Holdings, Tudor Brown, points out, "stock values are based on future earnings not present earnings". If the rewards are not likely to be as great as expected, some investors will choose to sell up.

The falls seen on stock markets over the past 24 hours would appear to have been triggered by the mid-term results. But concerns that tech firms have become overvalued were being expressed long before the elections.

The question now is whether this is simply the removal of froth from an over-exuberant market, or a sign that the AI rush is a bubble about to burst, with much wider consequences.

Nandini Roy Choudhury of Future Market Insights thinks investors will assess whether the political shift could result in restrictions on data centre construction, energy consumption and the deployment of AI technology.

She adds there is unlikely to be an immediate widespread recovery in tech stocks as traders are likely to be more selective, favouring firms with stronger balance sheets.

Brown thinks the impact will be limited. Share valuations, he thinks, were inflated by expectations of "almost infinite AI growth", which have been followed by "a bit of a panic".

"There is a natural floor to this", he says. "After that it will reflect I think that actually there's still a lot of money being made in these companies".

articles.title: Estas son las nuevas fechas de los debates electorales del 29N: La Sexta confirma el viernes 13 de noviembre para el primero
articles.standfirst: El periodo de quince días de campaña electoral para las elecciones generales del 29 de noviembre arrancará la próxima semana
articles.summary: El periodo de quince días de campaña electoral para las elecciones generales del 29 de noviembre arrancará la próxima semana
articles.body: Las elecciones generales del 29 de noviembre, como aquel que dice, están a la vuelta de la esquina. Un camino para saber cómo será la composición del Parlamento y del Senado en la nueva legislatura, además de saber cómo será la aritmética para conocer quién formará el nuevo Gobierno de España. Una decisión que tomará el país próximamente y sobre la que tiene mucho peso los diferentes debates electorales. Unos debates electorales que tendrán lugar de diferentes formas y maneras repartidos en las cadenas de televisión del país, como han acordado sus representantes políticos previamente y que se organizarán todos en los 15 días de campaña electoral que establece la Ley Electoral. La Sexta será la primera que celebre un debate para las elecciones generales del 29N. Será un debate a cuatro y tendrá lugar el próximo viernes 13 de noviembre, en pleno arranque de la campaña electoral. En esta ocasión los representantes de los cuatro principales partidos debatirán sobre vivienda y economía. Aunque el inicio del programa será a las 21:30 horas, el debate no iniciará hasta las 22:00 horas. Un debate en el que ya hay confirmados quiénes serán los políticos que estarán presentes. Pablo Bustinduy, de Frente Amplio; José María Figaredo, de Vox; Juan Bravo, del PP; y Carlos Cuerpo, del PSOE serán los que estarán en la mesa junto a la periodista y moderadora Ana Pastor. El martes 10 se procederá a hacer el sorteo de los turnos de intervención. Sobre el papel, el enfrentamiento de mayor voltaje de toda la contienda será el que tenga lugar el lunes 16 de noviembre. Un debate que organiza Mediaset España con una emisión simultánea en Cuatro y Telecinco. Se trata del único cara a cara pactado en una televisión privada hasta la fecha entre Pedro Sánchez y Alberto Núñez Feijóo. Empezará a las 22:00 horas. A medida que se acerca la cita, el choque entre los dos principales líderes políticos de España seguirá ganando tensión: los populares exigen amarrar la cita de Mediaset condicionándola al marco global de acuerdos, mientras que desde el entorno socialista aceptan el cara a cara del día 16 pero lo vinculan directamente a la celebración del debate a cuatro en la televisión pública. Sea como fuere, ambos parecen estar confirmados. Siguiendo la exigencia legal y la doctrina de la Junta Electoral Central (JEC) respecto a la proporcionalidad de las distintas fuerzas políticas, la radiotelevisión pública ha reservado el inicio de la última semana de campaña para este encuentro plural. El PP ya ha dado su visto bueno a la fecha y al formato, diseñado para analizar con un abanico más amplio de partidos la gobernabilidad y los pactos tras el 29N. En esta ocasión serían los portavoces de los ocho grupos con representación en el Congreso de los Diputados los que debatan entre sí. Todavía no se ha confirmado, por lo tanto, quienes serán los encargados de debatir y confrontar sus diferentes ideas de país. Lo que sí se sabe es que sería a lasortavoces de los ocho grupos con representación en el Congreso de los Diputados.. Es el punto donde encallan actualmente las negociaciones entre los comités electorales. El PSOE insiste en que el debate multipartidista decisivo debe celebrarse en RTVE. Por el contrario, el Partido Popular ha rechazado acudir a la cita en el ente público cuestionando su neutralidad y exige que este debate a cuatro se traslade a Atresmedia (emisión en Antena 3, laSexta y Onda Cero). Aunque todavía no hay confirmación, este debate se pretende que siga la continuidad de horarios de los anteriores y sea a las 22:00 horas del jueves 26 de noviembre. En él se contaría con los líderes de las cuatro principales formaciones: Pedro Sánchez por el PSOE, Alberto Núñez Feijóo por el PP, Santiago Abascal por VOX y Ada Colau por el Frente Amplio.

articles.title: Trump DOJ appointee who led ‘grand conspiracy’ probe of Trump foes resigns
articles.summary: WASHINGTON — The Donald Trump appointee who headed the office running a so-called “grand conspiracy” investigation looking into federal law enforcement officials who were involved in prior investigations of Trump has resigned.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The Donald Trump appointee who headed the office running a so-called “grand conspiracy” investigation looking into federal law enforcement officials who were involved in prior investigations of Trump has resigned. Attorney General Todd Blanche made the announcement on X Friday that U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Florida Jason A. Reding Quiñones had submitted his resignation, the second high-profile resignation at the Justice Department this week following massive midterm losses by Republicans. Blanche said they were “grateful for Jason’s leadership in combatting violent crime, drug trafficking, sex trafficking, and transnational crime, including the indictment of Raúl Castro” and that he had “served the Department multiple times over his distinguished career, and we thank him for his service to this country.” In his own post on social media, Reding Quiñones wrote that he was leaving “with immense pride in what we accomplished together and profound gratitude for the opportunity to serve our great Nation.” The “grand conspiracy” probe was seeking to charge officials over conduct that happened more than 10 years ago, based on the theory that separate investigations into Trump were part of a broader conspiracy against Trump’s rights. It sought to tie actions dating back to the 2016 campaign to the more recent Jack Smith investigation, which led to now-dismissed charges against Trump over seeking to overturn his 2020 election loss as well as his handling of classified documents found during a 2022 search of Mar-A-Lago. Trump denied the charges. No charges had yet been brought directly in connection with the “grand conspiracy” effort. Stacey Young, a former Justice Department lawyer who heads the group Justice Connection, said that “Jason Reding Quñiones will forever be known as this president’s Don Quixote for tilting at the windmill of the so-called grand conspiracy,” and that his “departure follows the well-tread path of others who signed up for this impossible dream.” Whoever replaces Reding Quñiones “should heed the great Attorney General Robert Jackson’s wise counsel that prosecutors should select those cases in which ‘the offense is the most flagrant, the public harm the greatest, and the proof the most certain,’” she added. Joe diGenova, who worked under Reding Quiñones in the Southern District of Florida, resigned in September, and blamed officials from Justice Department headquarters with stepping in and trying to take over the investigation. “Everybody was in their lane, and then some lanes got crossed, and then I decided to leave,” diGenova told NBC News. The Justice Department has recently brought charges against other Trump political foes, but hasn’t had much success in the effort so far. A judge dismissed a case against two former FBI officials who House Republicans accused of lying to Congress. The administration also recently failed to indict former White House official Cassidy Hutchinson, a star witness for the Jan. 6 committee. Harmeet Dhillon, the head of the Civil Rights Division which attempted to bring the Cassidy case, resigned on Thursday. Federal prosecutors are also seeking to bring a case against former FBI Director James Comey over conduct that allegedly happened in October 2016, when the government claims he authorized subordinates to speak to a New York Times reporter about national defense information. A separate case against Comey — related to an Instagram photo of seashells that the Trump administration contends was a threat against Trump’s life — is still pending in the Eastern District of North Carolina.
